articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont has confirmed that it will host a virtual “Pros and Cons” forum for a public discussion of ballot Measure UU on Wednesday, October 14, at 6:00 p.m. The measure is a proposed bond for $19.5 million to rebuild the City’s swimming pool at the existing location. The forum will feature a question and answer period for representatives in favor of and in opposition to the ballot measure and will be broadcast live on The Piedmont LWV YouTube Channel. Speaking in favor of the measure will be Betsy Andersen, a member of the City Council. Speaking in opposition will be resident Andy Wasserman, whose statement in opposition is in the voter handbook as part of the official ballot arguments. The public is invited to submit questions to be answered during the forum by emailing lwvpiedmont@gmail.com. The forum will begin with each side giving a two minute to opening statement, followed by a question and answer session. Each side will have one minute to answer each question. Each side will then be permitted to present a two-minute closing statement This will be the only ballot measure addressed during this forum. The opponents to Measure TT, increasing the Real Property Transfer Tax on home sales, declined to participate. According to LWV’s rules, both sides must agree to participate for the League to host a public forum. Questions may be submitted anonymously on the LWV website at: www.lwvpiedmont.org/ content.aspx?page_id=4002&- c l u b _ i d = 6 01 3 8 9 & i t e m _ id=1297116 The LWV of Piedmont’s Youtube channel will stream the virtual forum at: www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg

articles.text: Editor: Unfortunately, I missed the first Zoom discussion by the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. We moved to the City 52 years ago, and I researched its history as much as possible. Our home was built in 1919. But I found no more information in the City or County offices. I know the area around the spa was developed by wealthy San Franciscans as a summer resort. By many it was called a Millionaire’s Enclave. Segregation was caused by money. [The city] was always expensive, not only for blacks but whites also. I came from Europe 60 some years ago and was unfamiliar with racial differences or maltreatment of people different from me. But I learned it while living here. Ten or 15 years ago the black maintenance man of our office building occasionally came up to help me in our home. Every time coming or going, he was stopped by the Piedmont Police with some lousy excuse. No more. The City has changed a lot during this half century, particularly after the Oakland fire when a lot of younger people moved here. The past is past. Piedmont was segregated and the present sky-high property values, mostly in several millions in my opinion, does not make it a good prospect for the development of affordable housing. –Nicholas D. Molnar
articles.title: Piedmont may not be a good target for affordable housing

articles.text: Over the last few weeks the topic of housing equity in Piedmont has been the subject of community conversations, most notably via the information forum entitled, “Racial Segregation and Housing in Piedmont: How Did We Get Here? What Can We Do About It?”. In my review of recent articles, the discussion of the current housing realities included links and references to the history of Sidney Dearing, dubbed the first Black man to live in Piedmont. I first learned of Sidney Dearing on June 12th during a gathering in Piedmont Park when a number of people marched from the Wildwood Avenue area to the park to hear from a few speakers, most notably, young student speakers. It was at that event, I happened to be standing next to a woman who had material and signage with Sidney Dearing’s name and information. I was curious so I introduced myself and asked the woman to tell me about Sidney Dearing. The woman was Meghan Bennett and the history she recounted that day intrigued me and led to further review of her informative website that is dedicated to the Dearing/Piedmont history. I learned that the Department I lead had been on the wrong side of history. Others in the community have recently written about this history and I encourage people to read about it and visit the website. As a person of African descent, the information unfortunately was not surprising to me. As the Chief of Police of the Piedmont Police Department, it was ironic. As a professional law enforcement organization, it is this current-day Piedmont Police Department’s duty to understand this history, own it, and ensure we demonstrate an aptitude to be on the right side of history as we move forward. After learning of Ms. Bennett’s website, each member of the Piedmont Police Department had a conversation with me to review the site and discuss it. The conversations were interesting, introspective and cathartic. The power of the history of Sidney Dearing, from my perspective, is the specificity and tangible nature it attaches to what can sometimes seem abstract to some. This City, this police department, and members of this community did specific reprehensible things to this man to run him out of town because he was Black. To sit with current-day staff from the police department and for us to look at each other and talk about this history was impactful. This begs the questions, “So what?” and “What is the Department going to do that is different or impactful?” A number of years ago, President Barack Obama established the President’s Task Force on 21st Century Policing which developed guidance pertaining to progressive policing practices focused on building trust and legitimacy with the public, training, technology, policy formation, and officer wellness. articles.text: Editor: Three renowned infectious disease epidemiologists and public health scientists, Dr. Martin Kulldorff, professor of medicine at Harvard University, Dr. Sunetra Gupta, professor at Oxford University, and Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, professor at Stanford University Medical School, have authored an opinion about the best policy to control COVID, called “Focused Protection” dated October 20, 2020. The text is at: https://gbdeclaration.org/. “Current lockdown policies are producing devastating effects on short and long-term public health. The results (to name a few) include lower childhood vaccination rates, worsening cardiovascular disease outcomes, fewer cancer screenings and deteriorating mental health – leading to greater excess mortality in years to come, with the working class and younger members of society carrying the heaviest burden. Keeping students out of school is a grave injustice.” Keeping these measures in place until a vaccine is available will cause irreparable damage, with the underprivileged disproportionately harmed. “The most compassionate approach that balances the risks and benefits of reaching herd immunity, is to allow those who are at minimal risk of death to live their lives normally to build up immunity to the virus through natural infection, while better protecting those who are at highest risk. We call this Focused Protection.” Over 6000 medical and public health scientists and over 12,000 medical practitioners have signed this declaration. Please read the dcument, and if you support it, sign it as a member of the general public. With enough support, it could influence the current Bay Area COVID policies. –Bernard Pech Piedmont resident 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 922-8711 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Barry Eitel Allyson Aleksey Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: What is Measure UU? Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. How much will Measure UU cost? Measure UU would allow the City to issue up to $19.5M in 30-year fixed rate bonds. Measure UU will cost 2.6 cents per $100 of assessed home value (NOT market rate value). For the median Piedmont home, this works out to less than 75 cents a day. To look up your assessed value, use this link to the Alameda County Assessor’s Office and enter your address: http://acgov.org/MS/ prop/index.aspx What happens if Measure UU does not pass? When the 56-year-old Piedmont Pool is permanently closed, there will be no local swimming pool for residents or for Piedmont students. Piedmonters will have to travel and pay to use other communities’ pools, or pay initiation fees and annual dues for private swim clubs. With an empty padlocked pool facility in the center of town, the City will then have to decide what to do with that space. It is important to note that while the City decides, there is a cost to securing the site from blight and vandalism, as well as a significant cost associated with any future use of that space, whether it be for a pool or for some other use. Measure UU is a local Bond Measure which will provide funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable community pool for Piedmont families, students, and adults of all ages. Why is Measure UU needed? Built in 1964, the Piedmont Community Pool is well past the end of its useful life and needs to be replaced. Not only are there serious safety issues (on more than one occasion the concrete deck has failed and crumbled into the pool), the locker room facilities are outdated and restrooms do not comply with the Americans with Disability Act (ADA) requirements, the decades-old plumbing is failing and the pool leaks approximately 3,000 gallons of water daily – over a million gallons a year. Without the Piedmont Community Pool, Piedmont would be the only city (and only public school district) in Alameda County without access to a local pool. What will Measure UU funds do? The successful passage of Measure UU ensures that the Piedmont community will continue to have its own local pool facility for school sports/PE programs, lessons, and recreation, for the next 50 years. The cost includes planning, architectural fees, legal fees, demolition and construction for two new pools, restrooms, locker rooms, and community space. The three existing pools will be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. articles.text: Ordinance becomes effective on Nov. 4 At its meeting on Monday, October 5, Piedmont’s City Council approved a comprehensive sidewalk vending program. The city’s staff recommended the approval of a second reading of Ordinance 757, which allows sidewalk vending in compliance with California’s Senate Bill 946. It amends Piedmont’s current provisions that regulate sidewalk sales and other forms of mobile vending within the city. At its September 21 meeting, the council approved the first reading of the ordinance. Since then the ordinance has been available on the city’s website. No public comments have been received by the City Clerk’s office since the first reading. The ordinance goes into effect on Wednesday, November 4, 2020. The new ordinance allows sidewalk vending subject to the vendor obtaining a vending permit issued by the Piedmont Police Department. The city for many years has required all people selling door-to-door to first obtain a sales permit from the police department. Under the new ordinance, a sidewalk vendor must provide valid identification, proposed hours and days of operation, proposed location, type of merchandise to be sold, a valid seller’s permit, proof of a valid Piedmont business tax certificate, and any other information as may be required by the police department. The ordinance does not include guidance on food truck vendors.

articles.text: Piedmont must have its Measure A1 base allocation housing application approved by Alameda County in roughly 14 months, by December 31, 2021. The Alameda County bond, passed in 2016, allotted Piedmont $2,188,170 to create affordable housing. In the four years since its passage, Piedmont has not committed any of those funds toward affordable housing, but is currently exploring options. The measure was discussed during the newly formed Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign’s (PREC) first forum. Panelist Gloria Bruce, Executive Director of East Bay Housing Organizations, detailed the effect of the Measure A1 Housing Bond in Piedmont. It passed with 73 percent of the vote countywide, but only 52 percent of Piedmonters voted yes on the measure. The forum, which focused on housing equity in Piedmont in an ongoing series that explored a charge of systemic racism, prompted some residents to wonder why these funds are still untouched. Piedmont has made insufficient progress toward creating low-income housing, according to the California Department of Housing and Community Development. The city has a built-out quality with minimal space for new development, unlike neighboring cities that have quickly utilized the bond funds. Piedmont’s status triggers Senate Bill 35 (SB 35), which encourages cities to create housing on their own or be forced to accept housing developments. SB 35 aims to address the state’s housing shortage by increasing supply, and was signed into law in 2017 by former Gov. Jerry Brown as part of California’s 2017 Housing Package. The city’s housing element goals are to produce 38 affordable units by the end of 2022. On August 17, 2020, the City entered into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to research incentives for the construction of accessory dwelling units, or ADUs, that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable to very low and low-income residents. LWC is tasked with identifying potential sources of funding to support local incentives for the construction of income-restricted ADUs, and Measure A1 could be a potential source for funding. There may be other uses for funding identified through public engagement for the Senate Bill 2 housing programs or public engagement for the Piedmont housing element update. Senate Bill 2 provides up to $160,000 to plan projects that would streamline development of new affordable housing. “These funds must be used for projects which are affordable to very low and low-income residents for 55 years or more, as well as other restrictions and terms. The City has been discussing the options for using the Measure A1 funds with County staff, staff in other jurisdictions, as well as Habitat for Humanity,” said Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell . “The City would like to find ways to help fund the construction of ADUs, using Measure A1 or other sources.” In addition to the base allocation funding, City of Piedmont residents and employees are eligible for countywide Measure A1 programs, such as the AC Boost programs offered through the county for first-time homebuyer assistance for emergency responders and educators, as well as the AC Renew home repair program for eligible residents. The AC Boost brochures are posted on the city’s website and can be found by visiting https:// piedmont.ca.gov/cms/one.aspx ?portalId=13659823&pageId =16745183.

articles.text: • Amends the Existing Real Property Transfer Tax Should the Piedmont City Code be amended to increase the existing real property transfer tax to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price? Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale. In the City of Piedmont, the tax is currently at the rate of $13.00 per $1,000 of the value of the property The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that minimum additional funding of approximately $850,000/ year for the next five to ten years is needed to maintain the condition of city buildings, parks, streets and sidewalks. Measure TT would generate around $948,462/ year. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used A “YES” vote on Measure TT would be in favor of increasing the real property conveyance tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “NO” vote on Measure TT would be against the increase in the real property conveyance tax and would maintain the current rate of Opponents Say: The proposed increase of the City’s Transfer Tax rate would make it the highest flat rate in the entire State of California and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. There are no safeguards to ensure that the money from this tax will be directed to repair and maintain city facilities and that means the tax can be used for anything including salaries, pensions or project over runs. Piedmont already has an extremely high transfer tax rate. Increasing it will set a bad precedent in the region and could adversely affect homeowners that wish to sell their home in order to move into a retirement community. articles.text: Authorizes the City to Issue Bonds to Reconstruct the Piedmont Community Pool 2/3 vote needed to pass THE QUESTION Should the City of Piedmont be authorized to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of improvements for the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas? THE SITUATION The existing Piedmont Community Pool opened in 1964 and is now in its 56th year. The usual lifespan of most outdoor pools is 50 years. Prior to closure due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place orders, the City was spending approximately $1,000 a day to keep the pool safe and operational. The City believes that residents rely upon the Piedmont Community Pool as a resource to learn to swim, exercise, compete, play, and socialize. It has also been a steady source of employment for local youth. Based on a July, 2020 Concept Study, the estimated cost for replacement of the Piedmont Community Pool including bath house, pools and surrounding site work is $18.8 million. THE PROPOSAL If adopted, Measure UU would authorize the City of Piedmont to issue up to $19.5 million in general obligation bonds to finance the costs of replacing the Piedmont Community Pool and adjacent areas. It is proposed that the three existing pools be replaced with two pools to meet resident needs: a warmer recreation pool with areas for safe water play, swim lessons, therapeutic swim, and physical rehabilitation; and a wider and deeper pool for recreation, physical education, water aerobics, water polo, swim team, and lap swimming. The new pool facilities, restrooms, and related areas would conserve energy and water, comply with state and federal disability and safety standards, and provide restroom access for those using the tennis courts. FISCAL EFFECTS: If all of the bonds were issued and sold, the best estimate of the total debt service, including the principal and interest is $37,446,788. A “YES” vote on Measure UU would be in favor of authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool . A “NO” vote on Measure UU would be against authorizing the City of Piedmont to issue general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $19,500,000 for the purpose of constructing improvements to the Piedmont Community Pool Supporters Say: The pool needs to be replaced or it will be permanently closed. Measure UU provides necessary funds to construct a safe, sustainable, and affordable facility to serve Piedmont families, students, and seniors for the next 50 years. Passing this bond measure this year means taking advantage of historically low interest rates and avoiding continued escalation of construction costs in the future. Without the pool, Piedmont would be the only school district in Alameda County without a local pool for swim lessons, P.E, and water sports. Opponents Say: Piedmont should not be taking on $20 million of general obligation debt in the midst of fiscal uncertainty resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic. Oct. 14, 6:00 p.m. to - 6:30 p.m. at www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg Measure TT: Amends the Existing Real Property Transfer Tax Majority of votes required to pass THE QUESTION Should the Piedmont City Code be amended to increase the existing real property transfer tax to $17.50 per $1,000 of transfer price? THE SITUATION Real Property Transfer Tax (RPTT) is a one-time tax levied on a property at the time of sale. In the City of Piedmont, the tax is currently at the rate of $13.00 per $1,000 of the value of the property transferred. This rate was set in 1993. The Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee has recommended that minimum additional funding of approximately $850,000/ year for the next five to ten years is needed to maintain the condition of city buildings, parks, streets and sidewalks. FISCAL EFFECTS: Measure TT would generate around $948,462/ year. Funds generated by the proposed tax increase are not restricted and may be used for any City general revenue purpose. A “YES” vote on Measure TT would be in favor of increasing the real property conveyance tax to the new rate of $17.50 per $1,000. A “NO” vote on Measure TT would be against the increase in the real property conveyance tax and would maintain the current rate of $13.00 per $1,000. Supporters Say: The transfer tax is assessed only on property when it is sold, so it will affect relatively few residents each year. The proposed increase in the Transfer Tax rate will provide necessary funds for maintaining and improving city facilities, streets, sidewalks, and parks. The current transfer tax rate is significantly lower than Berkeley or Oakland and the increased rate would be lower than Berkeley and Oakland for some property sale values. Support – Signers of official arguments/ rebuttals: Robert S. McBain - Mayor Teddy Gray King - Vice Mayor Bill Hosler - Chair, Budget Advisory and Fin. Planning Committee John Y. Chiang - Former Mayor Chris Kwei - Member, Budget Advisory And Financial Planning Committee Opponents Say: The proposed increase of the City’s Transfer Tax rate would make it the highest flat rate in the entire State of California and could cost homeowners tens of thousands of dollars when buying or selling their home. There are no safeguards to ensure that the money from this tax will be directed to repair and maintain city facilities and that means the tax can be used for anything including salaries, pensions or project over runs. Piedmont already has an extremely high transfer tax rate. Increasing it will set a bad precedent in the region and could adversely affect homeowners that wish to sell their home in order to move into a retirement community. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. articles.text: This year’s Piedmont Education Foundation Giving Campaign has been overwhelmed with the positive response to the Giving Challenge that was announced last week. The Co-Chairs and the Foundation Board together have pledged to match, dollar for dollar, all new contributions to the Giving Campaign made between October 5 and October 19, up to $200,000. “We received such an amazing response after the match was announced. Gifts and pledges started coming in right away, and people were so happy to be able to double the impact of their gift,” said co-chair Colleen Allen. Some Giving Campaign donors are just learning that there are many ways to give. According to Foundation Executive Director Heather Frank, the Giving Campaign works to provide as many options as possible for families. It accepts checks, credits cards, and stock transfers, and gifts may be made through payroll deduction or donor advised funds. Pledges can be made now and paid off over time. “An increasingly popular option is to set up an automatic bill pay with your bank to send checks made out to PEF on a monthly or quarterly basis,” says Frank. “This allows our donors to pay off a pledge over several months and has the added benefit of eliminating credit card fees.” Frank also encourages everyone to learn more about their company’s matching program. Each year thousands of dollars are donated from companies that provide matching grants to their employees. Individuals are encouraged to check with their company’s HR department to learn more about the program. To help Piedmonters maximize their Giving Campaign donations and to better understand charitable deductions, Ludo Thomasson, a CFP and Wealth Manager and PUSD parent, is offering a short question and answer session on Friday, October 16 at 12:30pm. Registration is free and available at https://bit.ly/33Hh8CL. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, October 14, 2020 SchOOLs S P E E C H , I N C . “Productive Struggle” makes better learners By Katie Pengilly In the education literature, the term “productive struggle” refers to the process of effortful learning that develops grit and creative problem-solving. Neuroscience research shows that deep, lasting learning is achieved through productive struggle. To tap into this learning phenomenon, we need to emphasize the effort over the correct answer. Smart brains are efficient brains. When a student learns a skill or concept, myelin is produced, making brain signals faster and stronger. Challenging tasks which require cognitive struggle increase the production of myelin. Although challenge and struggle may make the learning feel more difficult in the moment, it is a difficulty that pays off in the long run. We can think about learning as a continuum, with surface learning at one end, and deep learning at the other. An example of surface learning would be a fact that is memorized for a test the next day. This can create an illusion of knowledge, yet this surface learning tends to dissipate, and may not be able to be retrieved for a future application to a new situation. On the other end of the continuum, we have deep learning, or mastery. Deep learning is enhanced by productive struggle, and results in conceptual understanding and procedural fluency with the new skill that is transferrable across situations and persists over time. For example, by adding some heavy lifting such as “show/discuss/ explain your work”, rather than simply produce a correct answer, the element of struggle and effort required can led to more durable learning. Both educators and parents can respond to incorrect answers by asking back questions which narrow the area of struggle, but do not entirely remove the struggle by giving the correct answer. Techniques to enhance productive struggle can be included in the classroom as well as at home. In the class setting, students called on who may not have the correct answer. Within a safe and supportive environment, students can be given time to explore and tinker with their ideas, alone or in a pair or group. Assessments can include expression and discussion of ideas and reasoning, the challenge/struggle of which will contribute to enhanced knowledge and retrieval, as opposed to a more passive multiple-choice format which tests a student’s ability to simply recognize a correct answer. At home, praise can be given for perseverance, or being able to express, discuss or explain a concept. Parents can encourage the child to apply curricular items to personal, meaningful experiences. Mixed practice can be encouraged at home, which may seem counterproductive, but due to the productive struggle which it creates, significantly improves long term performance. Simply highlighting and modeling our own reasoning process can also be educational. By making learning environments which value the “productive struggle”, in additional to enhancing specific learning, we are also teaching our children the life skill of embracing, rather than being made uncomfortable by, a challenge. We are teaching our children to enjoy the effort, starting with being intrigued by and learning from our mistakes. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech, Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at pengilly.katie@gmail.com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. articles.text: City recommends to avoid trick-or-treating this year The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) declared traditional trick-or-treating to be a “high-risk” activity for COVID-19 transmission, even with precautionary measures such as sanitizing and social distancing. Although trick-or-treating is primarily an outdoor activity, a statement issued by ACPHD Public Information Manager Neetu Balram said that it would be difficult to maintain a safe distance on porches and doorsteps. Instead, the health officer is encouraging community members to focus on decorations, and to limit activities to household members only. ACPHD also encourages virtual costume parties in lieu of in-personal socialization. “Trick-or-treating is a highrisk activity because it increases contact with people outside of your household who may not be as careful about COVID-19 prevention. Parties are high-risk, because mixing among people who don’t live in the same home introduces more opportunities for the virus to pass from one person to another,” Balram said. The department is still encouraging the use of masks, frequent sanitizing, and social distancing. Costume masks are not a substitute for protective cloth masks, but “avoid wearing a costume mask over a protective cloth mask because it can be dangerous if the costume mask makes it hard to breathe,” Balram added. Alameda County residents are reminded that local and state health officer orders are still in effect. Halloween gatherings, celebrations of Dia de los Muertos, and events or parties with non-household members are not permitted unless they are conducted in compliance with local and state health orders. Activities that are not permitted and are considered very high risk are crowded parties, haunted houses, and indoor mazes. Low-risk activities are recommended by the county, to include visiting an outdoor pumpkin patch, carving and decorating pumpkins outside, and preparing traditional family recipes with members of your household. The risk of traditional trickor-treating can be mitigated from high-risk to moderate-risk, if children participate in one-way trickor-treating where individually wrapped goodie bags are lined up for families to pick up and go while continuing to socially distance. The County also recommends that everyone participating should bring a hand sanitizer, use it frequently, and wash hands immediately after coming home. The Piedmont Police Department echoed the Alameda County recommendations. “The bottom line is that the city is recommending that people do not engage in high-risk behavior such as trick-or-treating,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers said.
articles.title: County says trick-or-treating is high-risk for COVID transmission

articles.text: Community invited to make scarecrows for Halloween Scarecrows from last year’s Harvest Festival set the tone for creativity and simplicity. To make autumn a little more festive, the Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers are putting on a socially-distanced Scarecrow community art and maker event. Families and pods are invited to make scarecrows for their front yards. This year’s theme is California Dreaming because we could all use a little optimism and creative cheer. To participate, make a scarecrow with your family or pod and have it in your front yard by Saturday, October 24. Post a picture of your scarecrow on your Facebook or Instagram page and tag #PiedmontScarecrowWalk2020. The Piedmont Arts Fund and Piedmont Makers will be posting scarecrows on their Instagram and Facebook pages. How to make a Scarecrow P ie d mont Ma ke r s ca n help. Need some inspiration on design? The Piedmont Arts Fund has some scarecrow inspiration on their Play Scarecrow Bingo with website: https://piedmontartsyour family f u nd.org /upcoming- events/ Print out the Scarecrow Bingo scarecrowwalk. card that will be posted on Sunday, October 26. Then take a Scarecrow Walk through Piedmont and fill out your card. Bring your completed card to Mulberry’s Market between October 26 and October 31 to receive a Scarecrow treat (limit one per person). Have an old Scarecrow in the basement? If you have an old scarecrow in your garage or basement, pull it out, dust it off, and give it a little California spirit. Everyone is welcome to participate.

As recommended by the state and county, Piedmont’s School Reopening Plan requires all school employees returning to campus to receive a COVID test the week before school resumes. 50 percent of the employees will receive additional COVID tests every two weeks on a rotating schedule. Students are not required to receive tests according to the plan. This was a point of concern for a few parents and staff who called into the school board meeting on October 6. The county and state’s position is that tests need to be saved for individuals who have been exposed or have symptoms. Piedmont mom Christine Schooley offered her observations as a teacher in Oakland. “I teach at a school in the flats that has the highest rate of COVID in the county for students and families. I ask that Piedmont, as a group, for the greater, save testing for those who really need it and who don’t have access. We can do this without our families rushing to require testing that gives a false sense of security for our students.” Each day before going to school, all students and staff must fill out a screening form for COVID symptoms. Checking off any item on the screening form requires at least 48 hours of quarantine at home. Items include: new or worsening cough, fever over 100 degrees, chills, diarrhea, nausea, and runny nose. At all times, everyone on campus must keep six feet from others, wear a mask, and wash their hands before entering a new room. There will not be on-campus lunch; hallways and entrances will be one way when possible. Plexiglass has been installed for teachers in classrooms. Teachers will have the right to dismiss any student not following safety requirements. Extensive cleaning will take place in all rooms and electrostatic sprayers will be used. Electrostatic spray is positively charged, allowing the appropriate sanitizers, mold preventatives and disinfectants to wrap around and evenly coat all types of surfaces for a more complete clean. All classrooms have been equipped with new MERV-13 filters on the heating and air conditioning units. Doors and windows will be open as indoor and outdoor conditions safely permit. “The idea is to use a variety of prevention techniques with the recognition that they won’t be able to be implemented perfectly all of the time by everyone, but in combination they should be very protective,” said Pearson. Children’s Fairyland Outdoor Park - Now Open Fairyland opened its Fairy Gates on Saturday, October 3. To ensure safety, puppet shows, Toddler Storytimes, live performances and rides have been put on pause. All tickets are reduced to $8. The slides are open, along with most Storybook sets. Meet at the beach or carpool from Piedmont available. Classes consist of 10-12 per stable pod for kids aged 5-12, masks and social distancing are required throughout. Guests will be able to experience the house like never before, with ample space and time in each room. Tour the 160 rooms at your own pace in your space. The Mansion Tour ticket also includes access to the Victorian Gardens. A nighttime flashlight tour is also open this month for Halloween. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. If Measure UU does not pass, the city will likely begin a process to permanently close the pool and determine alternate uses for that site. 2 – Budgets are a reflection of a community’s values. Public Safety, including crime prevention, wildfire prevention and disaster preparedness, is a top priority for Piedmonters. Over two-thirds of Piedmont’s General Fund budget is spent on personnel costs and two-thirds of the city’s personnel are police and fire personnel, consistent with our community’s values. We ensure efficient use of public funds and budget oversight with support of the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee (BAFPC), a tremendous asset to City Council and residents. As a former member, I found my colleagues on the committee to be smart, hard-working, dedicated financial professionals who offer comprehensive, detailed analysis and recommendations. The work of this committee has provided independent budget oversight, transparency and in-depth understanding of city finances. By implementing recommendations of this committee the city consistently strengthens its financial position. The BAFPC has consistently identified insufficient funds available to support the years of deferred maintenance the city has accrued which cannot be funded through existing General Fund revenue sources. Current ballot Measure TT will provide the necessary funds to begin to address this shortage. CONNIE HERRICK 1 – I’ve talked with several hundred residents during this campaign. The one issue that is on everyone’s mind is our community pool. I strongly believe we need to replace our pool. It is over 20 years past its usable life and beyond repair. Once the project is funded through Measure UU, a citizen’s committee will be formed to determine the best design. I hope for an energy-efficient facility that can easily accommodate all our sports, fitness, recreation and community gathering needs. I believe we will always reap significant returns on an investment we make in our health, wellbeing and community. 2 – Yes. We have gorgeous parks and a large variety of trees, carefully chosen and placed by our Parks Commission. Our streets, sewers and sidewalks are all extraordinarily well maintained. There is no emergency our Public Works Department can’t handle. Our Recreation Department provides a wonderful selection of community activities to support our health and well-being. Thanks to our Police Department, we enjoy a higher level of safety compared with our neighboring cities. Our Fire Department arrives within minutes to aid with emergency health or property issues. City staff and the volunteer efforts from all our other commissions/committees keep our City running smoothly. Given all the diverse challenges our City faces, we are doing a good job maximizing public funds. CONNA MCCARTHY 1 – Public safety and emergency preparedness are primary, overlapping, compelling issues. We must evaluate Piedmont’s essential services buildings to bring them up to current codes and standards. We must engage the community to measure interest, support and understanding of financial implications. On the list of many inadequacies, our existing fire facility is too small to accommodate current fire apparatus and equipment. Oversight is critical to efficiency. Piedmont residents have access to budget information and can critique or applaud what their decision-making bodies are doing. I served on the Municipal Tax Review Committee, (now Budget Advisory and Financial Planning). It is tasked with reviewing financial projections, funding and expenditures. Following the June 2020 review of the City’s annual budget proposal, proposed funding and expenditures from several long-term funds, and proposed midyear budget adjustments, the BAFP committee concluded: “Piedmont’s Finance Director was very thorough dealing with potential revenue risk, projected pension costs, OPEB funding, equipment replacement, and facilities maintenance. If Measure TT passes, the city will have the necessary funds so we can begin to address decadeslong deferred maintenance of our over 20 municipal buildings that are each 60-100 years old. Similarly, if Measure UU passes, the city will quickly begin a process of designing a pool facility that meets the aquatics needs of Piedmonters. The conceptual plan will be fully devel-

articles.text: sary supplies and services that they need. I would also work to make sure that we have a strong communication plan that would push messages to parents in three ways -- text, email and PUSD application notification. I would consult with [health] experts to make sure our numbers remain low and that tracing is completed when there are positive cases. I would also like to see a weekly dashboard of numbers and information available to parents and families JASON KELLEY 1 – Regarding schools, the single most compelling issue facing Piedmont right now is how and when we reopen in-person learning. The three groups of experts whose knowledge will guide us as we make decisions on this issue are: public health professionals, educators, and parents. Listening to these experts and finding consensus is the way forward. The plan now in place to open elementary schools incrementally is the result of much hard work and is a good beginning. As Alameda County hopefully begins to allow upper grades to return to school over the coming months, we should continue to listen to the concerns of both parents and teachers find the best way forward. 2 – In addition to the points outlined in my answer to the previous question, I think we also need to be working on instilling a sense of community responsibility among residents. Once schools have opened for in-person learning again, it will be everyone’s responsibility to make personal behavior decisions that will maximize the chances that the schools can stay open. That includes wearing masks and maintaining social distancing, not sending kids to school who have any symptoms are who are likely to have been exposed to anyone with the virus, and taking all the other steps recommended by public health experts to keep ourselves and our community safe. HARI TITAN 1 – I feel the most compelling issue facing Piedmont is continuing to earn the City’s reputation as an excellent place to educate our pre-K-12 kids. The median home value in Piedmont has risen to $2.2 million. Our additional school property taxes are still significantly lower than private school tuition. However, over the summer our response to Covid led some parents to temporarily move to areas that had in-classroom instruction. After a long back- and-forth and conflicting advice, this issue was recently resolved by the school board for elementary school. If I am elected, I will work to expand the parental choice of in-classroom instruction for middle school and high school as soon as we are allowed by county health officials and are prepared to move forward. As long as more families want to move here than leave, our home values will keep rising over the long term and all Piedmonters, including empty-nesters, will benefit. 2 – With in-classroom instruction resuming shortly, my biggest school safety concern is compliance with the school district’s mandates for wearing masks and social distancing as well as truthful reporting of health status at the beginning of each school day. This social contract needs 100% compliance for access to school grounds. I would offer to conduct school safety summits with parents to answer questions live and focus my risk assessment presentation to convince as many parents as possible of the importance of this compliance. Another idea is to utilize a School Resource Officer (SRO) in a proactive strategy designed to prevent compliance violations and also to intervene when non-compliant persons need to be removed from school grounds. This is totally in the scope of the SRO program which was developed to address juvenile crime and safety concerns in our local schools. SROs are typically tasked with maintaining a safe, secure, and orderly learning environment for students, teachers, and staff. CORY SMEGAL, Incumbent 1 – Of course, coping with the pandemic is the most challenging current issue. And while this will likely further impact school funding, our constant constraint, Piedmont has the opportunity to be a leader in addressing student well-being. Every year the District works to understand how our students are doing -- not just academically, but also from a social-emotional perspective. We survey our students once a year and not surprisingly, they are feeling stressed, they aren’t getting enough sleep, and many are just “doing school.” I am sure this hasn’t improved during the pandemic. The Board has recognized that this is a major issue. We held a Board workshop on student stress. We also purposefully updated one of our strategic goals to change the emphasis from achievement to engagement. We want our students to participate in relevant learning experiences that will foster life-long curiosity and that will spark creativity and promote collaboration. 2 – On October 6th, the School Board unanimously approved an approach for reopening that will phase in hybrid learning for our students, starting with our students with special needs and continuing with our youngest learners on November 3rd. Our plan covers the important aspects under the school’s control such as cleaning, disinfection and ventilation, cohorting, PPE, health screenings for students and staff, and testing, as well as rules for physical distancing and movement within the schools. As a Board member who helped shape these plans, I believe my role is to evaluate performance regularly and communicate clearly with the community. Everyone needs to understand the safeguards that have been put in place. Just as important are the measures families can take to ensure we are successful -- wear masks at all times when not at home, and be vigilant about washing hands, social distancing, and limiting the number of contacts. VERONICA ANDERSON THIGPEN 1 – Our schools are a microcosm of the most compelling issues we face as a community. PUSD faces challenges with school climate and culture that need to be addressed. Narrow definitions around performance and what it means to be a successful student lead to stress or disengagement. Reliance on traditional historical narratives combined with little to no diversity create a feeding ground for misguided beliefs and bias. Likewise, for Piedmont. Historically defined as a closed community, Piedmont today should use its social and economic capital to stimulate inclusion. Despite the abundant diversity in Oakland and other nearby communities, diversity here remains elusive. Community advocates are working intentionally to create policies and raise awareness through public discourse. This longterm work must be supported if we are ever to realize the community of belonging that we envision. 2 – I would support efforts to communicate to families the protocols for operating schools safely. Families also need details about their options if they have concerns or health risks. I would want to ensure that communications with parents are consistent, clear and transparent, and I’d suggest the district create easy-to-read materials to help parents have conversations with their young children about how to be safe when they go back to school. I’d want to be clear that, depending on COVID risk, it may be necessary to revert to distance learning at some point. I would also want to have confidence in county protocols for testing and contact tracing to contain exposure if someone gets sick. We must clearly communicate these protocols to families so that they know what to expect.

articles.text: Why I support the Pool and Measure UU When the City took over operation of the pool in 2011, I was asked to help design how the pool would operate. The system we came up with generated twice as much revenue as other public pools and saved the City a lot of money. I spent over a thousand hours in that effort. I was motivated to do so for two reasons: I wanted to be sure the City’s operation of the pool was a success, and I was concerned that if the pool got too expensive, the City might lose interest in it. I brought those same concerns to the discussions that led to the current pool proposal. We need to build a pool that meets the needs of the schools as well as the rest of the community. Under the facilities sharing arrangement between the City and the schools, the schools get to use the pool just as the City gets to use the schools’ gyms and sports fields. We are the same taxpayers who would be called on to fund a commuting to practice; designed so the high school water polo and swim teams don’t have to practice at night or commute to other pools; designed so kids can both play and have swim lessons after school; designed so lap swimmers have room to swim their laps when they get home from work at night. It’s not too expensive. The bond measure is about financing, not cost. You can’t bid the project until you have detailed construction drawings and no one would pay to have those drawings done until they knew they had the financing and the project would proceed. The increased cost estimate from 2016, when the conceptual design was initially approved, simply reflects that it will be built at least six years later. You don’t have to issue or spend all the bonds that are authorized. The City Council didn’t prioritize the pool over public safety, by putting the pool on the ballot. The fact is our infrastructure is old and needs to be addressed. The pool is on the ballot because there

articles.text: Editor: What has always made me a proud lifelong resident of Piedmont is seeing how dedicated our community is to improving the city and the lives of our residents. Across the board, we all do our part to make sure Piedmont continues to be a vibrant, beautiful place to live, committed to the success of our children and the overall health of the city. So much of what we do is in service to others. Throughout the years the community has come together to keep our schools top notch, keep our city parks beautiful and to build fantastic sports fields. We do this for our neighbors today and to ensure we are a desirable place to live for future residents.
articles.title: Keep Piedmont flourishing – vote Yes on Measure UU

articles.text: Editor: I’ve worked as a real estate agent for 12 years in the East Bay. I can say with absolute certainty that we need a pool facility. Taking clients around Piedmont to introduce them to the community is one of my favorite parts of the job. While showing them the
articles.title: Piedmont’s pool – a Realtor’s perspective

articles.text: We are swimmers and non-swimmers; people whose families have lived here for generations and people who are newer to the neighborhood; we are former mayors, school board members, Piedmont school teachers, city commissioners, and every day residents; people with experience in real estate and project development and people who understand city finance; people with young kids and retirees whose kids have long since flown the coop. We volunteered to be on the Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee for one reason: we love Piedmont and believe a public pool is vital to what makes the town of Piedmont a great place to live. We believe rebuilding the community pool is a priority that Piedmont should commit to now because of these facts: 1. The current pool can no longer function. Keeping the existing pool open is not a realistic option. The pool is crumbling, unsafe, and leaks thousands of gallons of water daily. It has frequent breakdowns taking it out of service. The significant maintenance costs throw the City’s good money after bad. The pool is now closed, and, unfortunately, its permanent closure is inevitable. 4. The existing pool doesn’t meet the needs of the community. Built in 1964, when LBJ was President, the current pool doesn’t meet modern needs or homebuyer expectations. The existing pool isn’t big enough for all the residents who want to use it – team practices, lap swimming, recreational play, and swim lessons. Our kids have to leave town just to practice their sport, and adults can’t get their exercise in after a long day at work. The proposed design better serves the community with an attractive, functional civic amenity at an important location in the center of town. 2. The existing pool has been used by a broad cross-section of Piedmont residents for the last 56 years. Virtually every Piedmont kid has used the pool – at swim lessons, summer camps, PE classes, birthday parties, lifeguard training, school celebrations, Piedmont Swim Team, or in high school as student athletes on the PHS/MHS swim and water polo teams. Adults have enjoyed the pool with their families or used it for exercise, rehabilitation, or recreation. 5. This is the right economic time to build the pool. Despite global economic uncertainty, it is actually an advantageous time for municipal construction projects. Interest rates are at historic lows and borrowing money will probably never be cheaper. Construction costs may even be lower, depending on the economic environment. Our tax payments don’t start when we authorize the bonds, but only when the bonds are issued as needed for the project. 3. Without a functioning and safe pool, Piedmont will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t provide a pool for its community and schools. Piedmont realtors are emphatic that a public pool for school and community use is one of the municipal features most highly valued by families making a move. Like the other characteristics that make Piedmont such a desirable place to live, a safe and accessible pool for our residents and our schools will translate into higher property values. 6. This project has been carefully evaluated and considered by City staff and the City Council for over five years. There have been hundreds of hours of meetings with consultants, hearings before the Recreation Commission and City Council, and numerous staff reports. There are 18 documents on the City’s projects/community pool web page chronicling the City Council action and analysis since 2015. These include the master plan and the aquatics feasibility study led by the leading aquatics consultants, Counsilman-Hunsaker, who have completed more than 1,000 aquatics projects across the country of every size and complexity. Piedmonters who came before us invested in the infrastructure that helps make Piedmont the wonderful town that it is. We’ve all been the beneficiaries of that generosity and foresight. It’s now our time to make an investment in our community that will last for generations of Piedmonters to come. It’s time to rebuild a community pool that meets the needs of the whole community. Join us, the unanimous Piedmont City Council and School Board, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Piedmont Recreational Facilitates Organization, the Beach Parents’ Organization, the Havens Parents’ Club, the Wildwood Parents’ Club, the PMS Parents’ Club, the PHS Parents’ Club, and the Piedmont High School Boosters Club, in supporting Measure UU. Abe Friedman Cathy Glazier Sue Herrick Wayne Jordan Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee Valerie Matzger Nancy McHugh Sarah Meyjes Chad Olcott Sarah Pearson Neil Ruthven Jon Sakol Tom Sullivan Ken Taylor Cameron Wolfe, Jr.
articles.title: WHY WE SUPPORT MEASURE UU TO REBUILD PIEDMONT COMMUNITY POOL

pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2020 11 POOL LETTERS MAIN Why I support the Pool and Measure UU By Jon Sakol When the City took over operation of the pool in 2011, I was asked to help design how the pool would operate. The system we came up with generated twice as much revenue as other public pools and saved the City a lot of money. I spent over a thousand hours in that effort. I was motivated to do so for two reasons: I wanted to be sure the City’s operation of the pool was a success, and I was concerned that if the pool got too expensive, the City might lose interest in it. I brought those same concerns to the discussions that led to the current pool proposal. We need to build a pool that meets the needs of the schools as well as the rest of the community. Under the facilities sharing arrangement between the City and the schools, the schools get to use the pool just as the City gets to use the schools’ gyms and sports fields. We are the same taxpayers who would be called on to fund a school pool. It’s time to have one facility that works for everyone – a pool designed so the Piedmont Swim Team doesn’t have to rent additional space in other communities and spend hours a week commuting to practice; designed so the high school water polo and swim teams don’t have to practice at night or commute to other pools; designed so kids can both play and have swim lessons after school; designed so lap swimmers have room to swim their laps when they get home from work at night. It’s not too expensive. The bond measure is about financing, not cost. You can’t bid the project until you have detailed construction drawings and no one would pay to have those drawings done until they knew they had the financing and the project would proceed. The increased cost estimate from 2016, when the conceptual design was initially approved, simply reflects that it will be built at least six years later. You don’t have to issue or spend all the bonds that are authorized. The City Council didn’t prioritize the pool over public safety, by putting the pool on the ballot. The fact is our infrastructure is old and needs to be addressed. The pool is on the ballot because there already was a plan to deal with the pool. The public safety issues just came up, there isn’t a plan to deal with them yet. The question is simple: does Piedmont want a pool or not? If we do, it makes no sense to build an inadequate pool. It’s time to have a community pool that finally meets the needs of the whole community. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure UU. Keep Piedmont flourishing – vote Yes on Measure UU Editor: What has always made me a proud lifelong resident of Piedmont is seeing how dedicated our community is to improving the city and the lives of our residents. Across the board, we all do our part to make sure Piedmont continues to be a vibrant, beautiful place to live, committed to the success of our children and the overall health of the city. So much of what we do is in service to others. Throughout the years the community has come together to keep our schools top notch, keep our city parks beautiful and to build fantastic sports fields. We do this for our neighbors today and to ensure we are a desirable place to live for future residents. For this reason, I passionately support Measure UU to rebuild the Piedmont Community Pool. The rebuilding of our pool is a necessity. not a luxury. Our pool is almost 60 years old, has passed its useful life and is now closed. We need to pass Measure UU for those who use the pool daily to exercise, for the children learning to swim and the young athletes who depend on the pool for training and competition. If Measure UU does not pass, we will be the only city in Alameda County without a local city pool. The pool has had such a positive impact on our community over the decades. That is why, on November 3, we must pass Measure UU, The community pool is one important piece of the overall big picture to keep Piedmont flourishing. –Adrienne Krumins Piedmont’s pool – a Realtor’s perspective Editor: I’ve worked as a real estate agent for 12 years in the East Bay. I can say with absolute certainty that we need a pool facility. Taking clients around Piedmont to introduce them to the community is one of my favorite parts of the job. While showing them the schools, we also go by the tennis courts, Rec Center, pool, and park. It looks lovely and convenient with all the recreational activities and classes conveniently located in a couple of square blocks of town. However, the buyers I work with are not just looking at Piedmont. The typical buyers are comparing a number of communities with good schools – including Orinda, Lafayette, Moraga, Marin, and Piedmont – all with the same question in mind. Where would we like to settle down and raise a family? A city is more than high performing schools and beautiful homes; it’s also the common areas and facilities that brings the community together. The other towns that buyers consider have beautiful city facilities and nice parks including several pools for schools and open to the public for recreation. The facilities through the tunnel are incredible, but there is no reason we can’t compete with their community offerings. Piedmont is known for its great schools both for their academics and athletics. The Piedmont High swim and water polo teams make up a large percentage of PHS student athletes. Without a local pool, Piedmont families will have to commute to other pools for their kids to practice and compete. I don’t know of another great public school that doesn’t have a pool. See Pool Letters on page 29 WHY WE SUPPORT MEASURE UU TO REBUILD PIEDMONT COMMUNITY POOL We are swimmers and non-swimmers; people whose families have lived here for generations and people who are newer to the neighborhood; we are former mayors, school board members, Piedmont school teachers, city commissioners, and every day residents; people with experience in real estate and project development and people who understand city finance; people with young kids and retirees whose kids have long since flown the coop. We volunteered to be on the Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee for one reason: we love Piedmont and believe a public pool is vital to what makes the town of Piedmont a great place to live. We believe rebuilding the community pool is a priority that Piedmont should commit to now because of these facts: 1. The current pool can no longer function. Keeping the existing pool open is not a realistic option. The pool is crumbling, unsafe, and leaks thousands of gallons of water daily. It has frequent breakdowns taking it out of service. The significant maintenance costs throw the City’s good money after bad. The pool is now closed, and, unfortunately, its permanent closure is inevitable. 4. The existing pool doesn’t meet the needs of the community. Built in 1964, when LBJ was President, the current pool doesn’t meet modern needs or homebuyer expectations. The existing pool isn’t big enough for all the residents who want to use it – team practices, lap swimming, recreational play, and swim lessons. Our kids have to leave town just to practice their sport, and adults can’t get their exercise in after a long day at work. The proposed design better serves the community with an attractive, functional civic amenity at an important location in the center of town. 2. The existing pool has been used by a broad cross-section of Piedmont residents for the last 56 years. Virtually every Piedmont kid has used the pool – at swim lessons, summer camps, PE classes, birthday parties, lifeguard training, school celebrations, Piedmont Swim Team, or in high school as student athletes on the PHS/MHS swim and water polo teams. Adults have enjoyed the pool with their families or used it for exercise, rehabilitation, or recreation. 5. This is the right economic time to build the pool. Despite global economic uncertainty, it is actually an advantageous time for municipal construction projects. Interest rates are at historic lows and borrowing money will probably never be cheaper. Construction costs may even be lower, depending on the economic environment. Our tax payments don’t start when we authorize the bonds, but only when the bonds are issued as needed for the project. 3. Without a functioning and safe pool, Piedmont will be the only city in Alameda County that doesn’t provide a pool for its community and schools. Piedmont realtors are emphatic that a public pool for school and community use is one of the municipal features most highly valued by families making a move. Like the other characteristics that make Piedmont such a desirable place to live, a safe and accessible pool for our residents and our schools will translate into higher property values. 6. This project has been carefully evaluated and considered by City staff and the City Council for over five years. There have been hundreds of hours of meetings with consultants, hearings before the Recreation Commission and City Council, and numerous staff reports. There are 18 documents on the City’s projects/community pool web page chronicling the City Council action and analysis since 2015. These include the master plan and the aquatics feasibility study led by the leading aquatics consultants, Counsilman-Hunsaker, who have completed more than 1,000 aquatics projects across the country of every size and complexity. Piedmonters who came before us invested in the infrastructure that helps make Piedmont the wonderful town that it is. We’ve all been the beneficiaries of that generosity and foresight. It’s now our time to make an investment in our community that will last for generations of Piedmonters to come. It’s time to rebuild a community pool that meets the needs of the whole community. Join us, the unanimous Piedmont City Council and School Board, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation, the Piedmont Recreational Facilitates Organization, the Beach Parents’ Organization, the Havens Parents’ Club, the Wildwood Parents’ Club, the PMS Parents’ Club, the PHS Parents’ Club, and the Piedmont High School Boosters Club, in supporting Measure UU. Abe Friedman Cathy Glazier Sue Herrick Wayne Jordan Community Pool for Piedmont Advisory Committee Valerie Matzger Nancy McHugh Sarah Meyjes Chad Olcott Sarah Pearson Neil Ruthven Jon Sakol Tom Sullivan Ken Taylor Cameron Wolfe, Jr. Vote Yes on Measure UU Paid for by the Friends of the Piedmont Pool – Yes on Measure UU 2020. articles.text: Richey recounts the time when he was ranked No. 1 in the U.S. A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s monumental sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. With the French Open now concluded, it’s a fiiting time to look back to a former top tennis tournament in the Bay Area: The Pacific Coast Championships. In the late 60s and early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world would gather in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the Berkeley Tennis Club and compete in the Pacific Coast Championship. One of the oldest sports events in the U.S., it was a top draw for major players from 1889 to 2013, it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States, predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of the Open era in professional tennis beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championship, 1969-1971, meant the best players in the world were close by. Many influential matches were taking place for the end-of-year rankings. An October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. Back in 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States in the semifinals of the PCC. It was one of the most memorable matches in the history of the sport. Their match lasyed more than “All the players, officials, or anybody who was close to the game knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an active spokesman for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. In his book, Acing Depression, Richey describes his challenges with the disease in the years following his tennis career. “It’s been a good book from the standpoint of what I wrote it for – to be able to help just one person. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts various amounts of time. It is a bonafide medical illness. In America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adam’s Apple down but not the Adam;s Apple up. It can happen to anybody,” Richey said. In the book he recounts some of his experiences with depression and what led to him write the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis on my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back. That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill. I had a three year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental-health book, with as desire to help others who Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of putting [the book] together It’s my tennis career and depression running on parallel tracks, meeting at the end,” he explained. . Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971,the final yearof the Pacific Coast Championship at Berkeley Tennis Club, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian performance with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues, starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. The Cow Palace and SF Civic Auditorium then hosted from 1973 to 1993 before it moved oto its final destination, the SAP Center in San Jose,; During its time it was in San Francisco, John McEnroe dominated the event with 14 combined singles and doubles titles – five in singles. four hours and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point as the end-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner to upset Smith, the favorite. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey, now 73 and living in San Angelo, Texas. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey about the match. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals in London. I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my butt was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals,in Berkeley in another epic match, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified the previous round. Photo courtesy of Berkeley Tennis Club Berkeley Tennis Club hosted the Pacific Coast Championships until 1971, featuring some of the world’s best tennis players. Photo courtesy of World Tennis Magazine Cliff Richey talks with the Post about his tennis career and mentalhealth activism.
articles.title: Tennis legend Cliff Richey & the Pacific Coast Championships at the Berkeley Tennis Club

articles.text: Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel won the NorCal Excellence tennis tournament in Manteca on September 2 against a group of highly rated players. Piedmont High senior Makenna Thiel, a ramked tennis player who has committed to the California Golden Bears next year, finished off the summer by winning the NorCal Excellence championship in the U-18 bracket. Competing from August 29 to September 2 in Manteca, she defeated some highly rated tennis players. Thiel opened with a 7-5, 6-4 victory over Esther Vrylan, a five-star rated freshman from Sacramento, then nearly double-bageled her next two opponents: Kate Sexton, 6-0, 6-0 and five-star recruit Gayathri Krishnan of Cupertino, 6-1, 6-1. “Excellence tournaments are the second highest level tournament. It was my second tournament since the start of quarantine,” said Thiel. “First round matches are always a little shaky, especially after not playing for a few months. I had to warm up in the first round, get a feel for the ball, and get back in match-mode,” said Thiel, a nationally rated prospect by the Tennis Recruiting Network. As an added incentive to her quick victories, it was her dad’s birthday on August 30. “The second day was my dad’s birthday and my sister said, ‘Get it done quickly so we can go home!’ I went out and probably played one of my best matches [against Krishnan]. My dad hasn’t been to one of my matches in some time, so it was nice to play well while he was there.” She defeated a familiar competitor, Tomi Main of R.L. Stevenson School in Pebble beach, 7-5, 3-6, 6-4 to win the tournament with th etemperaaature over 100 degrees. “I’ve been playing her (Main) quite a bit and we’ve always had competitive matches. It was very, very hot; our matches got delayed during the hottest part of the day. It was a battle,” she explained. Although the match was in the semifinal rounds, Maribella Zamarippa of St. Helena dropped out of the finals due to illness, elevating Thiel and Main to the championship round. The pair has squared off time and again, including in the semifinals of the 2019 NorCal Sectional Championships, which Thiel also won in three sets. “I didn’t feel necessarily fatigued at the end of it but I was so happy to be done with the match,” said Thiel with a laugh. “Maybe the adrenaline helped me out but I’ve been doing a lot of fitness to get through matches like those. It got me through.” With COVID causing changes in tournameen schedules, the match in Manteca was hher first since this summer. “It was my first tournament since June. I’ve just been focusing on practice because there are only so many tournaments in the area and I’m not really comfortable enough to get on a plane yet. There’s no need to rush around right now,” she said. A year from now, Thie will be among the headliners in Cal’s 2021 recruiting class after having committing to Cal in July. California’s 2020 recruiting class this summer included fellow five-star recruits Cami Brown of Irvine, Canadian champion Jada Bui, and Hannah Viller Moller of Denmark, meaning Cal could become the Pac 12 school y to keep an eye on in the coming years. Thiel is the Post’s 2019 Athlete of the Year after she won the North Coast Section Div. I doubles championship with Lauren Young. She was also the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2018 after helping Piedmont;s tennis team win its fifth straight North Coast Section team championship. Makenna Thiel defeated fellow five-star recruit Tomi Main to win a NorCal tournament. She also beat Main in last year’s NorCal Sectional semifinals.
articles.title: PHS senior Makenna Thiel wins NorCal Excellence tournament in Manteca

articles.text: The Piedmont School Board acknowledged in its recent meeting that Piedmont High School recently hired Bradley Smet, 29, as its new Athletic Director. He was one of vie candidates to be interviewed by staff and students in late September and appears to have been the favored choice of student-athletes. According to Piedmont School district’s press release, he was expected to start on Thursday, October 15, but he lives in San Luis Obispo and it was unclear if he already had moved to this area. As one of the youngest A.D.s to be hired in Piedmont, Smet comes with experience as both teacher and coach in the Atascadero School District. He was an assistant football coach at Templeton High and Atascadero High, is a former baseball coach at Atascadero High, and was a college quarterback at Sterling College, an evangelical Christian college in Sterling, Kansas. As a student at Atascadero High School, he led the Greyhounds as the starting quarterback on the football team and as a starting pitcher on the baseball team. Before attending Sterling College, he played on the football team at Hartnell College in Salinas. He graduated from Sterling College with a B.A. in History, and earned a Masters degree in Coaching and Athletic Administration from Concordia University in Irvine. The A.D. position at Piedmont has been vacant since the resignaBradley Smet has been hired as Piedmont High School’s new athletic director. tion of Alphonso Powell on July 24. Smet will be the high school’s fourth Athletic Director in five years.
articles.title: Piedmont hires Bradley Smet as new A.D.
