If the 49ers’ playoff chances continue to slide ahead of the Week 8 trade deadline, the front office could have a difficult decision on their hands. Shanahan has experience with two veteran QBs in the league: the Falcons’ Matt Ryan and the Vikings’ Kirk Cousins. It’s worth mentioning that the 49ers could save $25 million in cap space by cutting Garoppolo prior to the 2021 season. Lakers win 17th NBA Title Well, Warriors fans, going forward, it’s going to be a fierce rivalry in the Pacific Conference between the Lakers and Dubs. On Sunday, Los Angeles reeled in its 17th NBA Championship, a milestone also achieved by the Boston Celtics, after defeating the Miami Heat 106-93 and winning the playoffs 4-2 in a best of six games. Lebron James won his fourth Finals MVP and fourth NBA title after logging a triple-double: 28 points, 14 rebounds, and 10 assists. His large-and-in-charge counterpart, Anthony Davis, put up 19 points and 15 rebounds. For Lakers fans, it was a special sight after the passing of Kobe Bryant in January. Photo courtesy of Sports Illustrated Led by Lebron James, the Lakers won the organization’s 17th NBA title. The problem with making predictions is sometimes you’re proven wrong. The 49ers and Raiders did just that this week after San Francisco was unexpectedly demolished by the Miami Dolphins 43-17 while Las Vegas pulled off a major upset of the Super Bowl champion Kansas City Chiefs, 40-32. Starting with the winners, the Raiders are getting it done and becoming more difficult to predict each week. QB Derek Carr came to play; he completed 22 of 31 passes for 347 yards and three touchdowns. He looked more like the 2016 version of Carr, who at the time signed a five-year, $125 million contract. The Raiders’ pass rush, led by Clelin Ferrell, Maxx Crosby, and Arden Key, are proving to be a young underrated group. The team has a bye this week before facing Tom Brady and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 7. To beat the Bucs Vegas will have to provide another strong effort by their pass rushers. and limit playmaking receivers Mike Evans and Chris Godwin. The 49ers’ loss to the Dolphins is a definite cause for alarm. The team has lost two ina row to teams it was supposed to roll over. Its record has slumped to to 2-3, and it is in last place in the NFC West. San Francisco finds itself at a crossroad entering Week 6. With the LA Rams on the docket, SF will now be true underdogs for the first time all season. Although this writer is predicting a Rams win, the Niners could pull off an upset if its pass rush re-awakens with sacks and forced turnovers. Without defensive ends Nick Bosa, Solomon Thomas, and Dee Ford, the team is struggling. But its biggest struggle is at the quarterback position. Jimmy Garoppolo returned from injury in Week 5 only to struggle against lowly Miami, a team with identity issues of its own. He was 7/17 for 77 yards and two interceptions before getting sent to the bench at halftime. Although I doubt 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan and the front office is hitting the panic button just yet, the Red and Gold entering the trade market at quarterback could be a real possibility. The pair has squared off time and again, including in the semifinals of the 2019 NorCal Sectional Championships, which Thiel also won in three sets. “I didn’t feel necessarily fatigued at the end of it but I was so happy to be done with the match,” said Thiel with a laugh. “Maybe the adrenaline helped me out but I’ve been doing a lot of fitness to get through matches like those. By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont School Board acknowledged in its recent meeting that Piedmont High School recently hired Bradley Smet, 29, as its new Athletic Director. He was one of vie candidates to be interviewed by staff and students in late September and appears to have been the favored choice of student-athletes. According to Piedmont School district’s press release, he was expected to start on Thursday, October 15, but he lives in San Luis Obispo and it was unclear if he already had moved to this area. As one of the youngest A.D.s to be hired in Piedmont, Smet comes with experience as both teacher and coach in the Atascadero School District. He was an assistant football coach at Templeton High and Atascadero High, is a former baseball coach at Atascadero High, and was a college quarterback at Sterling College, an evangelical Christian college in Sterling, Kansas. articles.text: The CZU Complex Fire that waged in Big Basin Redwoods State Park of San Mateo and Santa Cruz Counties was contained in 37 days with an estimated 40 percent of its redwoods charred and 86,000 acres of the Along with the historic redwoods, the park’s headquarters building, constructed in 1936 as a WPA project, was destroyed. Additionally, the visitor center and campgrounds were burned. Big Basin is the oldest state park in California, dating to 1902. It contains and preserves some Redwood trees that date back more than 2,000 years. The park protects 35,000 acres of redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains, including approximately 10,800 of old-growth redwoods. The Peninsula Open Space Trust, a conservation organization, announced that a 9,000-acre preserve called the San Vicente Redwoods were destroyed. “For me, these were more than just ‘structures,’” said Walter T. Moore, president of the Open Space Trust. “They were places where we gathered for generations with our friends and families, places where we made memories and found ourselves surrounded by the splendor of the redwood forest.” He indicated that officials may not be able to fully assess the fire damage d for “months, if not years. But fire in this landscape can be healthy and beneficial for the redwood forest, which is very well adapted to survive fire. Fire is an integral part of this environment and helps to maintain the health of the ecosystem. Redwood trees, especially old growth, can withstand fire — and early indications are that many have survived,” he said. Last month, park officials said it could take a full year before Big Basin reopens. That sentiment was reiterated by Noelle Chambers Thurlow, Vice President of Peninsula Open Space. “It’s hard to answer when (the forest) will come back. We can only speculate. One year from now we’ll have a much better idea,” said Thurlow. “The fire was also a huge threat to farms in and around Pescadero and more broadly along the San Mateo County coast. Many of these farms operate on protected land and were evacuated with little warning. Forced from their operations for several weeks, their businesses suffered as they lost their ability to harvest and distribute their products,” added Moore. articles.text: Post sports writer runs into a bobcat It’s been a couple of years since our last visit to the Marin Headlands and Rodeo Beach, that bucolic, untamed stretch of land just past the Golden Gate Bridge. Last week we traveled far past Battery Townsley, bouncing around in and out of former military bunkers that date back to the 1930s. One of our destinations was Hill 88, a former military radar control station. The hike was 6.4 miles round trip and over 1,300 feet of elevation gain. After a brief closure of the parking lot near Rodeo Beach, park officials re-opened the area for hikers and beach goers. Given the popularity of the beach and first and last stopping point of Battery Townsley, you can expect to pass a lot of people at the start and end of your day. I passed 112 people on the day. One way to avoid lots of hikers would be to use the Coastal Trail bike path on the way up to Battery Townsley. Once you pass Townsley, keep an eye out for the trail sign that reads: “Wolf Ridge and Hill 88,” then continue up the Coastal Trail toward Hill 88. A smaller hillside bunker sits in the Marin Headlands. Keep an eye out for this trail sign after Battery Townsley. You can hop bunker to bunker up the hillside in the Marin Headlands. pages.text: Wednesday, October 14, 2020 15 HIKING WITH JON Bunker hopping in the Marin Headlands Post sports writer runs into a bobcat By Jonathan Comeaux It’s been a couple of years since our last visit to the Marin Headlands and Rodeo Beach, that bucolic, untamed stretch of land just past the Golden Gate Bridge. Last week we traveled far past Battery Townsley, bouncing around in and out of former military bunkers that date back to the 1930s. One of our destinations was Hill 88, a former military radar control station. The hike was 6.4 miles round trip and over 1,300 feet of elevation gain. After a brief closure of the parking lot near Rodeo Beach, park officials re-opened the area for hikers and beach goers. Given the popularity of the beach and first and last stopping point of Battery Townsley, you can expect to pass a lot of people at the start and end of your day. I passed 112 people on the day. One way to avoid lots of hikers would be to use the Coastal Trail bike path on the way up to Battery Townsley. Once you pass Townsley, keep an eye out for the trail sign that reads: “Wolf Ridge and Hill 88,” then continue up the Coastal Trail toward Hill 88. A smaller hillside bunker sits in the Marin Headlands. Keep an eye out for this trail sign after Battery Townsley. You can hop bunker to bunker up the hillside in the Marin Headlands. A view of Tennessee Valley Beach from a platform in the headlands. Ascending Hill 88, an abandoned military base on the other side of the Golden Gate Bridge. Hill 88 is an old radar control station. You can spot areas where aircraft used to land. The structures are open to explore. Photos by Jonathan Comeaux The view above Battery Townsley, the first of many former military bunkers around the Marin Headlands. From this point, you can easily venture around the headlands to separate yourself from other trail-goers. The Coastal Trail diverts in many directions; traveling northwest can take you to Tennessee Valley Beach – another trail we previously covered – or to a hilltop platform I sat on to take in the view of the headlands toward Mt. Tamalpais and the beach resting below. From that platform continuing west back on the Coastal Trail for a mile is Hill 88, which now is a graffiti-covered former military base where you can observe the peaks of the Golden Gate Bridge and San Francisco in the distance. It’s a good spot to rest and take in your surroundings after the ascent up after gaining over 1,000 feet in elevation gain in the time it takes you to get to Hill 88. You’ll pass a collection of two other former military bunkers on your way there, some with old sandbags that have hardened over time. The headlands are characterized by its open space with large fields of California poppies, coast rock cress, lupine, and monkey flowers. No matter where you are, you’ll see red tailed hawks soaring far overhead as they scan the ground for their next meal, often gophers. It was here that I had a shocking encounter with a fully-grown bobcat. Bobcat encounter Roughly 100 feet past the initial entrance of Battery Townsley is a second “gunner station,” which is directly across from the Wolf Ridge and Hill 88 trail marker. When exploring the open area on my own, a fully-grown bobcat ran away from the space I had just entered. Instead of snapping photos, I instinctively made my arms wide and shouted toward the wildcat. He ran without threatening me, but the sight was jarring given the amount of young children and dogs just hundreds of yards away. Local park rangers said that the sighting was considerably rare given that bobcats are nocturnal hunters. “To see a fully-grown cat at this time of day at that area is very rare. There have been some bobcat sightings in the past, but very seldom,” said a park ranger. Here are some guidelines for wildcat sightings: • Refrain from turning around and running. It shows fear, and an animal’s instinct is to chase its prey (that’s you). Back away slowly and deliberately get big. Spread your arms and be loud to scare the animal away. Inside the second gunnery station of Battery Townsley. Moments later, this writer had an unexpected encounter with a bobcat. Photo courtesy of Mercury News An encounter with a wild, fully-grown bobcat at Battery Townsley in the Marin Headlands.

articles.text: SF Ballet’s Jahna Frantziskonis is featured in Sequentia. San Francisco Ballet presents Sequentia, a choreographic chain letter to keep dancers and patrons connected during the global pandemic. Ten San Francisco Ballet dancers are connected through their movement in this choreographic chain letter. The film originated with a dancer who improvised a six-second solo to the music, and this choreography was passed along to the next dancer who picked up where the previous one left off. From the San Francisco Ballet, to New York City Ballet, to American Ballet Theatre, the “digital letter” started at the beginning of shelter-in-place restrictions and continues more than six months later through October in Seattle. In the video, patrons can view Pacific Northwest Ballet’s take on Seattle’s cityscape, working around and in-between the wildfires that have plagued the West Coast this year. San Francisco Ballet dancers who are featured include Tiit Helimets, Misa Kuranaga, Cavan Conley, Jahna Frantziskonis, Daniel Deivison-Oliveira, Myles Thatcher, Yuan Yuan Tan, Diego Cruz, Dores André, and Joshua Jack Price. The featured video for San Francisco is produced by Helimets and edited by Ben Estabrook. You can view the film on Youtube at https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=zhFuJEaVBtQ. articles.text: Bobak Cyrus Bakitiari (left) Johnny Moreno, and Jomar Tagatac star in the San Francisco Playouse production of Art. San Francisco Playhouse will premiere Art by Yasmina Reza on Saturday, October 24. The premiere will be streamed live and will be available to view for two weeks. The play explores how colleagues and friends can turn on each other when divided into opposing camps. There is a special focus on the complex layers of friendship, while at the same time maintaining a comedic tone. The play asks the question: Are we who we think we are, or are we who our friends think we are? Directed by Bill English, Art is translated by Christopher Hampton. It casts Bobak Cyrus Bakhtiari as Yvan, Johnny Moreno as Serge, and Jomar Tagatac as Marc. Reza is a French playwright and novelist based in Paris whose works have won many awards and received critical and popular international success. Art received the 1998 Tony Award and the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play. The London production of Art received the Olivier Award as Best Play in 1996. The original National Theatre production of Life x 3 also earned a 2001 Olivier Award nomination for Best Play. Her other noteworthy plays include After a Burial, The Passage of Winter, and The Unexpected Man. Theater fans can watch the video stream anytime between October 24 and November 7. There is a special focus on the complex layers of friendship, while at the same time maintaining a comedic tone. The play asks the question: Are we who we think we are, or are we who our friends think we are? Directed by Bill English, Art is translated by Christopher Hampton. It casts Bobak Cyrus Bakhtiari as Yvan, Johnny Moreno as Serge, and Jomar Tagatac as Marc. Reza is a French playwright and novelist based in Paris whose works have won many awards and received critical and popular international success. Art received the 1998 Tony Award and the New York Drama Critics Circle Award for Best Play. The London production of Art received the Olivier Award as Best Play in 1996. The original National Theatre production of Life x 3 also earned a 2001 Olivier Award nomination for Best Play. Her other noteworthy plays include After a Burial, The Passage of Winter, and The Unexpected Man. Theater fans can watch the video stream anytime between October 24 and November 7. articles.text: Writer and artist Chanel Miller will make her first museum debut, hosted by the San Francisco Asian Art Museum. Her exhibit, I was, I am, I will be, can be seen from the Hyde Street exterior of the museum. Miller was first known publicly as Emily Doe, the victim of sexual assault by Brock Allen Turner at Stanford University in 2015. The victim impact statement she wrote and read at her assailant’s sentencing hearing the following year went viral. It was read 11 million times within four days. The case gained international recognition because Turner, a 19-year old student athlete who raped Miller while she was unconscious, received only three months in jail. The case influenced the California legislature to require prison terms for rapists whose victims were unconscious. Judge Persky, who handed down the light sentence, was recalled from office by county voters in 2018. Miller’s memoir detailing the tragic event caught the attention of the Asian Art Museum’s head of Contemporary Art, Abby Chen. “Not only is she an amazing writer, she’s also this visual artist. But of course, she’s incredibly young,” Chen said. Chen and the museum staff began the process of collaborating with Miller. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum but never dreamed that one day she would be featured. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said, pointing to her art. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to shelterin-place orders, Miller’s exhibit was visible without even setting foot into the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. “The whole journey of healing is never linear,” Miller said, adding that she hopes the piece will be seen as universal and not confined to her particular experience. articles.text: Eugene Rodriguez (left), Fabiola Trujillo, Lucina Rodriguez, and Emiliano Rodreiguez of Los Cenzontles San Francisco Symphony continues its digital programming curated and hosted by Oakland Symphony conductor Michael Morgan in collaboration with San Francisco Symphony musicians and guest artists from the Bay Area. The Currents video series and companion podcast series is released every two weeks, and explores the intersection of classical music with four musical cultures, illuminating the connections and ways that cultures influence each other and evolve together. The last in the series of four, is Viva Mexico!, exploring Mexico’s multi-generational musical culture, and feature the music group Los Cenzontles (guitar, vocals, percussion). Maestro Morgan will introduce Eugene Rodriquez from Los Cenzontles, Bay Area musician and teacher Martha Rodriguez-Salazar, and San Francisco Symphony cellist Jill Rachuy Brindel, who describe how Mexican culture connects and transforms traditions while building community. “I am thrilled to be helping the San Francisco Symphony share all the wonderful things they do with a wider and more diverse audience. Within the symphony we have musicians with almost every musical interest. We just want to share our broad interests with our audience, old and new,” Morgan said. The episode will be released in conjunction with a podcast series, which aims to further elaborate on and personalize the conversations and themes introduced to its accompanying video episodes. Released the week following each video episode, the audio episodes provide additional opportunities to tie in current events, personal stories and perspectives. The Currents series includes performances and candid, personal reflections by members of the San Francisco Symphony. The complimentary podcast is hosted and curated by conductor Daniel Bartholomew-Poyser, who will explain the interactive activities at the end of each video. “We don’t want you just to listen. We want you to engage and respond to what you’re hearing in our Currents series,” he said. To view the performance, see: sfsymphony.org/currents. Free Delivery to Piedmont

articles.text: The first time I became fully aware of Ruth Bader Ginsberg was when I saw the Betsy West/ Julie Cohen documentary, RBG. It was revelatory. Here was a woman, an octogenarian, a justice of the Supreme Court, a progressive icon who has been for all of her professional life a frontline champion of women’s rights. Popularly known as the “Notorious RBG,” in recent years she had become diminutive, even fragile in appearance. She was often seen on an interview stage wearing her signature gloves, her mind resolutely incisive and keen, a figure embraced by the public’s imagination during a time fraught with divisive politics. In recent years she had health scares; cancerous nodules were excised from her lung. For the first time she was absent from the high court while following arguments at home. It is no exaggeration to say that her health challenges sent a shudder through the center-left political milieu; clearly her voice would be dearly missed. Made in 2018 the feature film On the Basis of Sex is a broad biopic that opens with RBG, played by Felicity Jones, as one of nine women in a class of 500 admitted to Harvard Law School. The year was 1954. At a dinner party the women are asked to explain to all gathered why they have chosen to “occupy a place at Harvard that could have gone to a man.” This question is proffered by Harvard’s Law School Dean (Sam Waterston) and proves to be startlingly tone deaf, though in keeping with the attitudes of the time. Still, Ruth perseveres. She is married to Marty Ginsberg (Armie Hammer) and the mother of a babe in arms. When Marty, a class ahead of Ruth at Harvard, is stricken with a serious illness, it is Ruth who attends his classes and her own, while keeping the home afloat. The film skips five years ahead to 1959. Now graduated, she is frustrated when work is all but impossible to find for a woman. It’s a male dominion. She ends up teaching law instead of practicing law, which was her closely held intention. In 1972 Ruth takes on what will eventually become a landmark legal case regarding sex discrimination. Ironically, the plaintiff is a man. As it turns out, Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsberg who passed away on September 18, 2020 is the subject of the film On the Basis of Sex. Ruth prevails and the outcome impacts sex discrimination law nationwide and launches her in a direction that neither she nor Marty could have anticipated. On the Basis of Sex is a nicely done tribute film, extolling the career of a woman of extraordinary talent and resilience. It is also a window into her life outside of the classroom and courtroom, unabashedly showing that RBG was fortunate to have had a caring, confident and generous man standing by her side. On the Basis of Sex. Starring Felicity Jones, Armie Hammer and Justin Theroux. Directed by Mimi Leder. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Felicity Jones portrays Ruth Bader Ginsberg in On the Basis of Sex. articles.text: Rose Byrne and Hugh Dancy in Adam. Moview review by Chris Honoré Call it a staple of Hollywood screenwriting: girl meets damaged boy. She is moved to reach out and care for him, perhaps rescue him in some fashion. Ditto for boy meets damaged girl. Incrementally and inextricably, both scenarios become matters of the heart and love is soon entangled with the impulse to help. As stories go, it’s instantly familiar but also ripe with new and interesting permutations. Adam, written and directed by Max Mayer in 2009 and nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival, is such a narrative. Beth (Rose Byrne), twenty-something, an aspiring writer of children’s books, having just escaped a disastrous love affair, moves into an Upper West Side brownstone. Living in the building is Adam (Hugh Dancy), an electrical engineer who designs toys and is also consumed with origins of the universe. When they first meet, in the laundry room, it is inescapable that Adam’s affect and responses are different. He doesn’t respond to the normal cues of conversation. Beth is intrigued for Adam is also bright and direct and sincere. What she soon learns is that his quirkiness is caused by Asperger’s Syndrome, a form of high functioning autism. Though she comes to understand how Adam’s Asperger’s presents itself, she also recognizes a lovely human being. In slow motion she falls in love with him and he with her. Beth also comes to understand that an aspect of the syndrome (at least in Adam’s case) is an inability to feel empathy, or make straightforward contact, such as looking her in the eyes. Adam hears what others say, but he is unable to feel the subtext behind the words or detect humor or irony. What is said, he takes at face value, even if a sentence ends with a question mark. Still, Beth moves forward, slowly involving Adam in her life, introducing him to her parents and to her friends. It’s not easy for her or for Adam. Adam is a small, sweet movie, wonderfully acted, and, to Mayer’s credit, explores both characters. Clearly, it was tempting to make this Adam’s story, but Mayer resisted. Hence, Beth’s ambivalence and personal qualities are nicely balanced with Adam’s struggles. As well, there’s a tangential story concerning Beth’s affluent parents (Amy Irving and Peter Gallagher): her father is on trial for embezzlement, the family uncertain if he will go to prison. Adam is a small nugget. Mayer has created a touching film that’s worth seeing. Adam. Starring Hugh Dancy, Rose Byrne, Frankie Felson, Peter Gallagher and Amy Irving. Directed by Max Mayer. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Adam a small gem from director Max Mayer

articles.text: A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Tale of Princess Kaguya. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Tale of Princess Kaguya is based on a 10th century Japanese folk tale called The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter. The film was written, directed and animated by the co-founder of Ghibli Studios, Isao Takahata. Though less known worldwide to his colleague Hayao Miyazaki, he is an equally gifted storyteller and animator, his talents made manifest with this Oscar nominated film. Princess Kaguya is, however, a departure from the vibrant hand-drawn animé that made the Studio Ghibli films coveted not only in Japan, but globally. The images of Princess Kaguya are soft, using a pale palate that is absent the full-frame insistence of primary colors. Instead, the animation is a blend of pencil, ink, and watercolor washes with restrained splashes of color. As well, its narrative tone is calm, subtle, telling the wonderfully imagined story of a middle-aged bamboo cutter (James Caan) who comes upon a strange stalk and finds enveloped inside a fully formed, elegantly dressed little girl (Chloe Grace Moretz), no bigger than a small sparrow. In amazement, he stands holding this small mystery-miracle cupped in his hands. He brings the tiny child home to his wife (Mary Steenburgen). Childless, they are overjoyed and embrace the foundling. What they soon find miraculous is that within weeks the tiny girl, who they regard as a heaven-sent blessing, grows into a beautiful young woman who finds joy in the natural beauty that surrounds her bucolic home. She plays with the neighboring children (a bit feral) and is drawn to a handsome farm boy (Darren Criss). Her parents, however, become convinced that this special daughter they call Princess is of noble blood and so take her to live in a mansion just outside the city, hoping a high society suitor will appear. And indeed, she is soon courted by five handsome Princes, who, as it turns out, cause her continued displeasure. She tells her parents that it is her wish to not marry. It soon is evident that the life she desires is in the countryside. Before long we see Princess Kayguya escape, running through the forest – a montage of rushing streams, enveloping flora and fauns – gripped by an anguished need to return to the life she had before and that special farm boy who only showed her kindness. The Tale of Princess Kaguya is whimsical, magical, while possessing a thread of melancholy throughout. Its story is one that is slow to emerge and may test the patience of a young American audience. But typical of the Studio Ghibli brand, it is lovely to behold. The Tale of Princess Kaguya (2014). Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Voices of Chloe Grace Moretz, James Caan, Mary Steenburgen and Darren Criss. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG. With Extended hours to Fit Your Busy Schedule Dr. Gutlaizer with Anne Marie O'Brien and daughters Aubrey and Anjuli and pets Zola and Zar

articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s UP. Film Review by Chris Honoré Like its Pixar antecedents – Ratatouille, The Incredibles, Monsters, Finding Nemo, Cars and the incomparable Wall-E – Up delights and entertains audiences of all ages. The animation is flawless, the attention to detail breathtaking. It’s the story a let’er rip adventure that takes a retired, squarefaced, bespectacled curmudgeon, Carl Fredricksen (Ed Asner), 78, and his uninvited sidekick, Russell (Jordan Nagai), 8, to the jungles of South America. As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer, Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. The only thing missing in his life is that one magnificent adventure he has dreamed of for years. Having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he and the house imply float away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of liftoff. And so the journey begins, with a most unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. Pete Docter and his team at Pixar used unbridled imagination and an enchanting story that captivates and entertains. Made in 2009, it won an Oscar as Best Animated Feature. The film even manages to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl’s uses that poignant aphorism that life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Animated with the voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar films. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG.
articles.title: UP – the finest from Pixar

As a young boy, sitting in darkened movie houses, watching newsreels of the famous explorer, Charles Munz, Carl dreamed of having a great adventure. One afternoon, walking home from the matinee, he meets Ellie who, he discovers, has exactly the same spirit. They grow up nurturing the belief that some day they will stand together in an exotic spot, surrounded by vast jungles and cascading waterfalls. Alas, life gets in the way and in a wonderfully crafted four-minute montage, Carl and Ellie’s life together is revealed: years quickly pass, countless moments of joy and sadness are shared. The only thing missing in his life is that one magnificent adventure he has dreamed of for years. Having lost Ellie, Carl is now living alone in their quaint house surrounded by high-rise buildings under construction. Carl refuses to sell and every day he is being buffeted by life and all its changes. In a moment of inspiration, Carl ties 20,000 helium balloons to the top of his house, forming a magnificent bouquet of colors, and early one morning he and the house imply float away. Unbeknownst to Carl, Russell, an earnest, well-equipped Wilderness Explorer, happened to be on his front porch at the moment of liftoff. And so the journey begins, with a most unlikely pair riding on the southerly winds, headed toward South America. There they will meet talking dogs; a very old Charles Munz; a large, chocolate-loving bird named Kevin; and take an unexpected ride on a vintage dirigible. Pete Docter and his team at Pixar used unbridled imagination and an enchanting story that captivates and entertains. Made in 2009, it won an Oscar as Best Animated Feature. The film even manages to work in a few life lessons for Carl and Russell. Carl’s uses that poignant aphorism that life is what happens while you are waiting to really live (and go to South America). UP. Animated with the voices of Ed Asner, Jordan Nagai and Christopher Plummer. Written and Directed by Pete Docter and Bob Petersen. Pixar films. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s The Tale of Princess Kaguya. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Tale of Princess Kaguya is based on a 10th century Japanese folk tale called The Tale of the Bamboo Cutter. The film was written, directed and animated by the co-founder of Ghibli Studios, Isao Takahata. Though less known worldwide to his colleague Hayao Miyazaki, he is an equally gifted storyteller and animator, his talents made manifest with this Oscar nominated film. Princess Kaguya is, however, a departure from the vibrant hand-drawn animé that made the Studio Ghibli films coveted not only in Japan, but globally. The images of Princess Kaguya are soft, using a pale palate that is absent the full-frame insistence of primary colors. Instead, the animation is a blend of pencil, ink, and watercolor washes with restrained splashes of color. As well, its narrative tone is calm, subtle, telling the wonderfully imagined story of a middle-aged bamboo cutter (James Caan) who comes upon a strange stalk and finds enveloped inside a fully formed, elegantly dressed little girl (Chloe Grace Moretz), no bigger than a small sparrow. In amazement, he stands holding this small mystery-miracle cupped in his hands. He brings the tiny child home to his wife (Mary Steenburgen). Childless, they are overjoyed and embrace the foundling. What they soon find miraculous is that within weeks the tiny girl, who they regard as a heaven-sent blessing, grows into a beautiful young woman who finds joy in the natural beauty that surrounds her bucolic home. She plays with the neighboring children (a bit feral) and is drawn to a handsome farm boy (Darren Criss). Her parents, however, become convinced that this special daughter they call Princess is of noble blood and so take her to live in a mansion just outside the city, hoping a high society suitor will appear. And indeed, she is soon courted by five handsome Princes, who, as it turns out, cause her continued displeasure. She tells her parents that it is her wish to not marry. It soon is evident that the life she desires is in the countryside. Before long we see Princess Kayguya escape, running through the forest – a montage of rushing streams, enveloping flora and fauns – gripped by an anguished need to return to the life she had before and that special farm boy who only showed her kindness. The Tale of Princess Kaguya is whimsical, magical, while possessing a thread of melancholy throughout. Its story is one that is slow to emerge and may test the patience of a young American audience. But typical of the Studio Ghibli brand, it is lovely to behold. The Tale of Princess Kaguya (2014). Directed by Isao Takahata. Animé from Studio Ghibli. Voices of Chloe Grace Moretz, James Caan, Mary Steenburgen and Darren Criss. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG. articles.text: One Fair Wage founder Saru Jayaraman, will speak and answer questions with Waging Change filmmaker Abby Ginzberg on Zoom October 14. Waging Change, a film by Abby Ginzberg, is a powerful, uplifting documentary about the long-shot campaign of Saru Jayaraman and her restaurant worker colleagues to oppose the powerful National Restaurant Association and its lobbyists in order to achieve a livable income for their work and to end the unfair tip-based system of payment. The Federal minimum wage for tipped workers is $2.13 an hour. For our screening of Waging Change, we’re trying a new format: Stream the film between October 9-18 at your convenience. articles.text: Music has had more than its share of comedians. Some, like Victor Borge, were just plain funny. Mozart’s humor was scatological. French composer Erik Satie was slyly societal. Richard Wagner was completely humorous. At the opposite end of the spectrum, was American composer Benjamin Franklin. Yes, you read that correctly… American composer Benjamin Franklin. While he was on diplomatic service in Paris, Franklin embedded himself into every manner of Parisian society. He was popular with the ladies even when he couldn’t even speak proper French. His scientific mind encouraged him to go to the violin shops and see the greatest bow maker of the time. This resulted in Franklin‘s invention of a most controversial musical instrument. The glass armonica became immensely popular for a while. It disappeared almost as fast as it appeared when it acquired the reputation that playing it could cause insanity. I know…it sounds crazy. Undeterred, Franklin investigated other areas. Chamber music was very popular among amateur musicians. Seeing a ready market, Franklin decided to become a composer. Readers should be aware that the string quartet medium is probably the most difficult medium in all of composition. But Ben was undeterred. He set about writing a string quartet. After all, he knew most of the great composers of the time. The first thing that he did was to invent a special tuning system for the four instruments. Once he did that, he knew success was his. Virtually anyone could play the Benjamin Franklin String Quartet. All the players needed to do was to tune their instruments the Franklin way. That was all. You see, with the Franklin system, you didn’t even need to put your fingers on the instruments. Calabrian-inspired fish I haven’t given a recipe lately, so here is one of my favorites. It’s easy to make and can be ready to serve in less than 10 minutes. Ingredients Opah (moonfish), tuna or trout Salt, Italian seasonings, red pepper flakes Avocado, marinated artichoke hearts, either roasted red peppers or dried tomatoes Starch - potatoes, polenta or bread Season the fish liberally with some salt, and Italian seasoning fortified with red pepper flakes. The fish should have some bite. Sauté the fish gently in butter. Top the fish with some slices of avocado. Serve on the same plate with marinated artichoke hearts, roasted red pepper or dried tomatoes, and potatoes, polenta or bread. Total cooking time from preparation to table is about eight minutes. Beverage: a light beer or an effervescent red wine complements the spice of the fish. For those who avoid alcohol, try some peach iced tea. Dessert is equally easy: iced coffee and vanilla ice cream. Piedmont Center for the Arts looks into the future While the Piedmont Center for the Arts has been treading water during the COVID crisis, I have good news. Piedmont’s cultural gem is making plans for an exciting future. Its history has been one of tremendous artistic diversity. It has welcomed art shows and art lectures. History has become enlivened by those who actually lived it. And music has set the pace. Some of the most important European concert artists are ready to set concert dates in the city’s lovely performing venue. They will be here at the first opportunity. I feel like I am back on the track team. The runners are at their mark… anticipating... Calabrian fish: Bright colors and lively flavors make Calabrian fish a winner. It’s very easy to make and takes obly about eight minutes.

articles.text: To attract more riders on their cable car line to Piedmont, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built a Bandstand for concerts, a Tea House, Maze, Venetian Canal and small amusements for children. As the Cable Company failed to make a profit and was going into receivership in 1893, they added balloon ascensions to attract more riders on their cable cars. Hot Air Balloon Ascensions There was always an element of excitement and danger with the hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park, and they drew many visitors. By 1896, there were balloon ascensions every Sunday and on the 4th of July. Balloonists were considered daredevils, and for 25 cents visitors could ride up with the balloonist. Most of the balloon ascensions at Blair Park were aerial gymnasts, “dressed in spangles and tights” and doing “hair raising” stunts on a trapeze suspended from a captive balloon. It was exciting to watch the balloon fill with hot air. Young boys were allowed to hold the anchor lines as the balloon filled. As the aerialist climbed into the balloon basket, the balloon handler ordered the boys to “Let Go!” Visitors watched in awe as the balloon rose over their heads. One particularly daring aerialist hung upside down from the trapeze bar as it ascended. After several acrobatic stunts on the bar, the aerialist finished with a parachute drop from a height of 1000 feet. The balloon was on a long tether, and the balloon manager pulled it back to earth at the end of the show. One Sunday a balloon ascension ended fatally. Little Bertram Hills was visiting Blair Park with his aunt in July 1897. He had been holding onto one of the sand bag anchor lines when the balloon began to rise. He failed to let go of the line and rose with the balloon - 300, 600, 900 feet up in the air. The tether failed. It was a terrible sight to see little Bertram dangling from the line and holding on for his life while balloonist Charles Conlon attempted to return the balloon to earth. Unfortunately, Bertram’s strength gave out before the balloon could descend, and he fell to his death. His body was found a half mile away on farmland in the Montclair hills. The public lost its taste for balloon ascensions in Blair Park after little Bertram’s death, and the ascensions in Blair Park ended shortly thereafter. What Became of Blair Park? As fine as the intentions of the park operators were, Blair Park seems to have encountered problems almost immediately. In 1892, the Oakland Tribune reported that “gamblers had things their own way up at Blair Park” and described prospering shell games. Citizens were also concerned that the planned casino would attract “scum and hoodlum.” In 1896 the Board of Directors of Mountain View Cemetery complained that “the balloon ascensions on Sundays from Blair Park is [sic] becoming a great nuisance, attracting a great crowd of the hoodlum element and causing a disturbance in the Cemetery Grounds.” They called on the Sheriff to protect the cemetery grounds and arrest trespassers. The fate of Blair Park was tied to the fiscal success of the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company. In 1892, electric trolleys were replacing the cable cars and competing for ridership. Due to the great expense of building the cable line, the Piedmont Cable Company went into receivership in 1893, and the assets were sold at auction in 1895. Walter Blair’s heirs continued to own the park land, but it was heavily mortgaged. In 1897 all of Blair’s 235 acres, including Blair Park, were for sale. Mountain View Cemetery bought 1-1/2 acres on the northern edge of the park. In 1901, the Cable Company announced that it was abandoning the park and that it would not reopen that spring. the Realty Syndicate owned the park land. The park was set for development. Throughout these last years, Blair Park continued to operate. Park, because the Blair family no longer owned the land. Charles Vosmer, one of the park’s balloonists, managed the park up to 1905 when its listing disappeared from city directories. The Blair Park land was still vacant in 1913 when the City of Piedmont, then six years old, voted to acquire land for parks. Voters approved the purchase of Dracena and Linda Parks, but not Blair Park. In 1917, new homes began to appear on the Blair Park site. Builder Guy Taylor built 11 bungalows on the north side of Moraga Avenue, both shingled and stucco styles. He returned in 1922 to build at least 6 more bungalows. As you drive along Moraga Avenue today, you can see the similarities that many of these homes share. Blair Park Today The early sketches show Blair Park in a grove of eucalyptus trees. Walter Blair thinned some of these trees to make paths and picnic areas. The Cable Company thinned more trees to make room for their attractions. Finally, more eucalyptus were thinned when the houses were built along Moraga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. There were cascading waterfalls in Blair Park in the 1880s. The stream that ran down Moraga Canyon is now in a conduit under Moraga Avenue. The canyon was filled for decades ultimately creballoon shaped sign is a reminder of the ascensions in the 1890s.

articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission conducts an annual Design Award Program to recognize Piedmont property owners who have done an extraordinary job of planning and designing their construction and landscaping projects. From a list of projects completed the previous calendar year, the Commission chooses a select number of superior designs that meet the City’s design and planning guidelines and exemplify the highest level of design excellence in the community. This year’s event was held on Monday, October 12 starting at 5:30 p.m. Aric Shalev and April Gruber, 74 Sea View Avenue, won Excellent Comprehensive Stylistic Transformation. Nicholas and Rani Batra, 17 Sotelo Avenue, won Excellent Landscape and Outdoor Living Area. articles.text: Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn is currently at the helm of the Piedmont Community Church following the retirement of Rev. Dr. Bill McNabb on September 20. Ashburn, the Associate Pastor, will serve as Acting Head of Staff until January 1, when the new Transitional Minister, Rev. Dr. Steve Schibsted, begins. Ashburn, who lives in Piedmont with wife Margaret and two children, has been with the church since 2003, Ashburn graduated from San Francisco Theological Seminary in 1997 and later earned a Doctorate of Ministry degree there in 2015. He now preaches on Sundays, teaches a Wednesday morning Bible Study by Zoom and leads a Friday morning Prayer Service. If filling in for McNabb after a celebrated 19-year career isn’t hard enough, Ashburn must do so via recorded video, audio and Zoom meetings. His first sermon was a week ago on October 4. Hampered by the invisible coronavirus, Ashburn has had to rely on the internet and Wi-Fi, to reach the church’s congregation of approximately 1000 people. “It is harder to preach in front of a camera than it is to preach in front of people,” Ashburn acknowledged. “I get my energy to preach from the people there in person. So now I have to generate it all for the camera. I have gotten better at it, and it is really good to be able to reach more people than just those in church on Sunday morning.” he said. Ashburn counts the work of the church’s Communications Director, Michael Barber, as a blessing. Barber puts together the digital audio and visual content on the PCC website. PCC’s sermons are recorded through Soundcloud at www.piedmontchurch.org/worship-podcasts/. The church is cautiously optimistic that in-person services may return in November. Rev. Dr. Don Ashburn is the Acting Head of Staff until Transitional Minister Steve Schibsted starts on January 1. “We have a task force that is working very actively on [reopening]. We have done as much preparation as we can. I think we can be ready when the time comes. Our top priority is making sure people are healthy and safe,” Ashburn confirmed. Ashburn expressed deep veneration for the work of McNabb. “[Bill] has gone off to this new horizon of retirement and left behind a good, solid basis on which we can do ministry. We will miss his gifts in preaching and commitment to the church’s involvement in its local outreach and mission.” Ashburn has known Schibsted for a few years and feels confident the church will be in good hands under his direction starting next year. “Steve has a good sense of humor and is very centered in his faith. I think he will make a really great difference at PCC. He is a really good guy,” Ashburn added. For now the church is focused on continuing its outreach to a community facing today’s unique coronavirus challenges. “I’m really optimistic. I think it is a really good time to try a bunch of new things to make the changes we need to make, while keeping the things we need to keep with integrity and faithfulness.” Our team is here to solve your plumbing, heating and cooling problems! articles.text: At an August 5 meeting the Piedmont Park Commission considered three types of trees as the official street tree for residents on Olive Avenue. After a lively discussion a winner was declared: the Purple-Leaf Plum. It beat out the others – Chinese Pistache, and the White Flowering Crepe Myrtle, currently on view in front of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Commissioners noted that Purple-Leaf Plums already on Olive Avenue were some of the best examples of the species in Piedmont. There are currently eight existing Purple-Leaf Plum trees on the same block. Purple-Leaf Plum trees, also called cherry plum trees or flowering plum trees, are small deciduous trees known for their dark red to purple foliage. The species is noted to be fast-growing, with low maintenance and little pruning. The commission was asked to choose a designated street tree at an October 7 meeting, and decide if the neighborhood would benefit from the uniform look of one species. Chair Patty Dunlap said that she would like the commission to explore the idea of a single species tree designation for the entire street. “The Plums are doing really well [in this location], and the neighbors had asked about a faster-growing tree. The plums fit that [request] to a pretty good extent,” she said. Commissioner Betsy Goodman wondered if there was a lighter colored Purple-Leaf Plum option. Parks & Projects Manager Nancy Kent responded that another type was lighter – bronze in color – but was rejected as an option. “I don’t think we can suggest a different variety of the Purple-Leaf,” Kent said. Dunlap supported the choice of Purple-Leaf Plums. “What I love is the elegance it adds, the rich color, and the continuity would really elevate that street and make it look pretty majestic,” she said. “It was a great process. We had a chance to go out into the community and make this selection. The city did their due diligence and their homework,” she added. The new trees could be planted before the end of the year. “Our Public Works team will take the lead on that. I think we’ll have them planted in about a month or so,” Kent said. Purple-Leaf Plum tree

articles.text: An orphaned mountain lion cub was rescued by Cal Fire firefighters on September 27 in the destructive Zogg Fire in southwestern Shasta County. The male cub was brought to Oakland Zoo to begin recovery and rehabilitation. Upon discovering the lone cub, Cal Fire notified the Shasta County Sherriff’s Department, who asked for guidance from the California Department of Fish and Wildlife [CDFW]. CDFW Veterinarians contacted Oakland Zoo for help in treating the young mountain lion. The young cub has been nicknamed “Captain Cal” as an homage to the fictitious Cal Fire mascot. The two share a strikingly similar story: mascot Cal also survived a wildfire and found a home with the firefighters who led the community to safety. Captain Cal is only four to six months old, “a small victim of climate change,” Veterinary Hospital Director Dr. Alex Herman said. He arrived at the Zoo at about 7 p.m. on September 30, driven from Redding by Pete Figura, Supervising Wildlife Biologist for the CDFW. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

articles.text: William V Hassenzahl Jr, the father of three children, passed away on October 10, 2019. He was 53. He was born on January 21, 1964 in Urbana, Illinois, the son of Jeanne and Bill Hassenzahl Sr. He attended Piedmont schools and graduated from Piedmont High School in 1983. An active member of the Piedmont Boy Scouts, he was an Eagle Scout in Troop 4. He was a Professional Engineer, with a Bachelor’s degree from CalPoly in San Luis Obispo. In 1999, he married Rene Rolin in their adoptive home town of Las Vegas. There they raised three daughters, Gillyan Elise, Madelyn Mae, and Antonia Jeanne. Bill grew up loving adventure. He was an avid skier and a ski patrol member, a skydiver and skydive instructor, and a bicyclist. He enjoyed and meticulously cared for his Viper and Kawasaki racing bikes and loved family getaways in the Utah mountains. He is survived and dearly missed by his parents, Jeanne and Bill Hassenzahl, a Piedmont grad in the class of 1983, died on October 10. He was 53. Bill Hassenzahl Sr., his daughters and their mother, his brothers David and Eric, many nieces, nephews, cousins, aunts, uncles and many personal and professional friends.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had another engaging book discussion on Zoom is October 5th. A strong turnout of 16 members of the group were on the call to discuss their October read, The Dutch House by Ann Patchett. The group was pleased to welcome Maya Rath, a first-time participant. City Councilmember Jen Cavenaugh was on the call, too. Regular members participating included Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Jeri Lockhart, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Karin Featherston, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Sally Arney, Sweeling Chen, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Dutch House is the eighth novel by Patchett, who has also written three non-fiction books. The readers agreed that she is a gifted writer. It was also noted that the book has been described as a modern fairy tale with elements of Cinderella, The Little Princess, and Hansel and Gretel. The book describes the life story two siblings, Maeve and Danny Conroy, and their family in “The Dutch House,” a 1922 mansion outside Philadelphia. Their father, Cyril, a successful real estate businessman, bought it at a 1946 estate sale as a surprise for his wife, Elna. The house was built by a wealthy Dutch couple and thus was given its name. However, Elna hates the house, both aesthetically and ethically. It is just too wasteful for her when the world has so many other needs. She flees the house and her family when the children are ten and three, ostensibly to go to India to devote herself to serving the poor. Mauve and Danny bond tightly after their mother leaves, but they and the family suffer; as if “they had all become characters in the worst part of a fairy tale,” as Patchett writes. Andrea, a pretty young widow 18 years younger than Cyril, falls in love with his house and manages to get Cyril to marry her. She and her two small daughters move into the house and the troubles for Maeve and Danny begin. After Cyril dies, their wicked stepmother forces Mauve and Danny out of the house in classic fairy tale fashion. The rest of the novel is their complicated life story, their relationship with the house, and their long journey back to it. The Dutch House was well received by most of the readers, but some had issues with the book, and thus made it an excellent book group selection. Some readers thoroughly enjoyed the novel. For them it was beautiful, charming, and entertaining. Mauve and Danny’s strong, supportive, sibling relationship was appreciated. Patchett’s character development of them and others made the story personal and enjoyable for the readers. The Dutch House is written in the first person from Danny’s adult point of view. Some readers felt Danny and his father were clueless about what the family was experiencing. Some members listened to an audio version of the book read by Tom Hanks, and loved his presentation and the emotions he conveyed in his reading. Some readers were not as satisfied with the book, saying that the story fell apart in Part III and at the book’s ending. They found many elements of the story unbelievable. Everyone seemed to agree that The Dutch House is a well-written fairy tale. The group previously selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for their November read and Jane Austen’s classic, Pride and Prejudice, for December. Some readers said they want to read Longbourn by Jo Baker, a story from the Pride and Prejudice servants’ perspectives. The First Monday Reading Group next meets on November 2, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration with the Recreation Department is required. For more information, contact John Wilk at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: MONDAY READING GROUP Monday Reading Group discusses The Dutch House

Regular members participating included Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Jeri Lockhart, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Margie Blodgett, Bella Almanzan, Karin Featherston, Albert Chen, Margie Blodgett, Sally Arney, Sweeling Chen, Dick Carter, and group leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The Dutch House is the eighth novel by Patchett, who has also written three non-fiction books. The readers agreed that she is a gifted writer. It was also noted that the book has been described as a modern fairy tale with elements of Cinderella, The Little Princess, and Hansel and Gretel. The book describes the life story two siblings, Maeve and Danny Conroy, and their family in “The Dutch House,” a 1922 mansion outside Philadelphia. Their father, Cyril, a successful real estate businessman, bought it at a 1946 estate sale as a surprise for his wife, Elna. The house was built by a wealthy Dutch couple and thus was given its name. However, Elna hates the house, both aesthetically and ethically. It is just too wasteful for her when the world has so many other needs. She flees the house and her family when the children are ten and three, ostensibly to go to India to devote herself to serving the poor. Mauve and Danny bond tightly after their mother leaves, but they and the family suffer; as if “they had all become characters in the worst part of a fairy tale,” as Patchett writes. Andrea, a pretty young widow 18 years younger than Cyril, falls in love with his house and manages to get Cyril to marry her. She and her two small daughters move into the house and the troubles for Maeve and Danny begin. After Cyril dies, their wicked stepmother forces Mauve and Danny out of the house in classic fairy tale fashion. The rest of the novel is their complicated life story, their relationship with the house, and their long journey back to it. The Dutch House was well received by most of the readers, but some had issues with the book, and thus made it an excellent book group selection. Some readers thoroughly enjoyed the novel. For them it was beautiful, charming, and entertaining. Mauve and Danny’s strong, supportive, sibling relationship was appreciated. Patchett’s character development of them and others made the story personal and enjoyable for the readers. The Dutch House is written in the first person from Danny’s adult point of view. Some readers felt Danny and his father were clueless about what the family was experiencing. Some members listened to an audio version of the book read by Tom Hanks, and loved his presentation and the emotions he conveyed in his reading. Some readers were not as satisfied with the book, saying that the story fell apart in Part III and at the book’s ending. They found many elements of the story unbelievable. Everyone seemed to agree that The Dutch House is a well-written fairy tale. The group previously selected Caste by Isabel Wilkerson for their November read and Jane Austen’s classic, Pride and Prejudice, for December. Some readers said they want to read Longbourn by Jo Baker, a story from the Pride and Prejudice servants’ perspectives. The First Monday Reading Group next meets on November 2, at 1:30 p.m. New members are always welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration with the Recreation Department is required. For more information, contact John Wilk at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. READ IT IN THE POST Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000. articles.text: Thigpen can allow school board to finally walk the walk Editor: Veronica…Finally! When I first read Veronica Anderson Thigpen’s bio several months ago, I was blown away with excitement. I don’t remember knowing any past candidate with her qualifications in education, creating policy, and helping school districts achieve their goals. Plus, she so instantly spoke to the issues we so urgently need to address that I felt a newfound sense of hope for our city and our children at this critical time in our history. In Veronica’s outreach, she even wanted to know how we citizens felt about issues in Piedmont Unified School District – how refreshing. Upon meeting her, I was further impressed by her natural sense of inclusivity as she listened closely to our concerns and spoke to our group. Finally, a wise, calm, super-qualified person of color can hold a political office on our school board. This is her time, I believe. Having had the privilege of teaching art at Wildwood Elementary for 20 years has allowed me to see that reaching students is way more than getting the lesson done; it’s more than test standards and test scores. Students need a level playing field, safety, empowerment, and a voice in order to establish the confidence to grow, be curious, and to love learning. Let’s not let a gem like Veronica Anderson Thigpen slip by. With Veronica, we can and not just talk the talk of equity in our schools. –Suzie Skugstad

articles.text: Editor: It’s time to vote for School Board seats and I recommend Hilary Cooper. I believe she has all the essential attributes of a successful, effective member of the board. She brings perspective, energy and commitment to our town and our schools. Over the last decade, she has: • Galvanized neighbors and community members to support our schools financially by spearheading two PEF Giving Campaigns • Led the Parent Boards of the Middle and High School • Partnered with administration and staff during leadership transitions, learning first-hand the players and the roles. • Been a liaison with the Wellness Center on the social/ emotional needs of our students • Succeeded in passing Measure G&H to secure critical local funding for our schools Her commitment to our schools and our kids is supported by her long record of success. Whether it’s funding, staffing, curriculum, student needs, parent concerns or community buy-in, she has the experience and drive to keep our schools great. I hope you’ll join me in voting for her for Piedmont School Board. –Doug Ireland
articles.title: Voting for Hilary Cooper to keep schools great

articles.text: Editor: We are writing in enthusiastic support of Conna McCarthy for Piedmont City Council. Conna’s life has been steeped in public service in every aspect of her life and, for years, she has volunteered her talents to Piedmont’s education and civic communities. The breadth of her knowledge and experience, her on-going commitment, and her candid approach will continue to serve us. Please join us in voting for Conna for City Council. –Amal & Rick Smith

articles.text: Editor: I am writing in support of Veronica Anderson Thigpen for election to the Piedmont School Board. Veronica will bring a dynamic new perspective to the board. Her professional, volunteer and life experiences make her an excellent candidate. Veronica moved to Piedmont from Chicago where she earned degrees in Economics and Journalism from Northwestern University. Veronica has authored award winning writings on educational policy, and currently advises school systems and educational nonprofits on building equitable and effective organizations. Upon arrival in Piedmont, Veronica eagerly joined our enthusiastic volunteer community and has made several important contributions. We are fortunate to have a candidate with such broad understanding of educational policy, and a willingness to share her talents and knowledge.

articles.text: Editor: Conna’s commitment to our community is obvious - through her participation on school parent boards, chairing of fundraising activities, service as Recreation Commissioner and spearheading of city campaigns. Conna thrives on creative problem solving and seeks out diverse opinions in order to find solutions. Her community interests range from school sports and civic programs to city beatification and the arts. And, I must add, her love for the Piedmont community is clearly evident in her vast purple and white wardrobe! Most inspiring, however, is the way Conna has prioritized service to others and instilled this value in her family. Whether serving our country, our community or vulnerable segments of the population, Conna, Peter and their children have all made career and volunteer choices that contribute to the greater good.
articles.title: McCarthy’s commitment to service and community

articles.text: Editor: Conna McCarthy has real leadership qualities. I have watched Conna in action in many volunteer situations. She listens, she is curious, she asks questions, she seeks many opinions. She understands there is a process and is not afraid to speak up and advocate for what she feels is right. She really knows how to build bridges and seeks the higher ground. She is a problem-solver and is the right woman for the job and future of Piedmont. Vote for Conna McCarthy for City Council. –Valerie Corvin
articles.title: McCarthy knows how to build bridges; seeks high ground

articles.text: Editor: I am proud to support the candidacy of Conna McCarthy for City Council. Her many years as a school and city volunteer, her experience in budgets and financial planning, and successful law career will stand us well in the complicated years ahead. She is a passionate but thoughtful advocate who will also listen. Piedmont’s City Council would be fortunate to benefit from Conna’s proven skills and lifelong commitment to service and giving back to her community. –Molly Waste Ashford

articles.text: Do buildings or pools have ‘life spans’? We say No. Most of the homes in Piedmont are much older than the Community Pool complex. Our homes are not obsolete. With proper maintenance, repair and updating of systems, our homes and the pool do not have ‘life spans’. Yet, the City Council has concluded that the community pool ‘life span’ is over. Even though the City Council has a Study, completed in 2018,* that concluded that the pool could be repaired and rehabilitated for a cost in the low millions and that the pool would be out of service for only about 6 months. Measure UU will require a 3-4 year shutdown and a $19.5 million price tag. There are several examples of this community’s ability to raise those sums for a project fairly quickly. The 2018 study concluded that “the pool vessels appear to be structurally sound”. Why then should we demolish every structure on the Pool site and start afresh at a site which is far from ideal with respect to parking, traffic congestion and impact on the neighborhood? In our opinion, the case for pool repair and rehab has not been fully explored or explained to the voters by Council or the proponents of UU. That is the major flaw in the logic for putting forth this Measure at this time. We consider it to be misplaced priorities. Is Measure UU the first and highest priority for the City? We have previously and continue to say No. The safety of our community should always be the highest priority. The structural upgrade of our Essential Police, Fire and City Hall Buildings should be the City’s highest priority at this time! In our opinion, this issue should preempt any decision about the scope, nature and the location of a community pool. Choosing repair and rehab of the pool complex now would give the City Council and staff the time – a breather if you will – to properly and prudently complete the extensive due diligence (schematic plans, environmental and traffic studies and good quality estimates, etc.) required on all of the major projects on the City Facilities Needs Summary. At that point an orderly and logical Capital Construction Plan could be implemented. We encourage voters to do some research on these very important issues, and we strongly urge a No vote on UU to create a timeout. That alone would allow for a proper planning and budgeting process. articles.text: Editor: Years have passed since our kids grew up. The splashing and playing are warm memories. The swim lessons are thankfully long past. There were the July 4th games for which the kids couldn’t wait. Looking ahead, we might occasionally swim laps in a new pool, which will provide a healthy outlet, and it will be wonderful to see a beautiful new facility, but our family is not likely to be a regular user. Rebuilding the pool facility will be expensive. So why support it? When we moved to Piedmont in 1996, the pool was there for us, as part of the City’s broad array of recreational facilities, and we made good use of it. It’s time to pay it forward. Like all Piedmont residents, we are proud of our town, and we want it to flourish in the future. We will be proud to do our share for the new pool. I have been on the Recreation Commission for almost six years, and its Chair for over half that time. Through the Commission’s broad dealings with recreation in Piedmont, there is one constant – the need for more and improved facilities. It would be incredibly unfortunate to reduce the facilities we have now. Please join us in supporting Measure UU. –Steve and Karen Roland
articles.title: UU and Piedmont’s pool. Time to pay it forward

articles.text: Editor: We are writing in support of Measure UU which will replace our decaying Piedmont pool infrastructure with two new pools – a larger pool for lap swimming and competitive sports and a much-improved recreation pool for shallow water play, swim lessons, and other water fitness programs. Located in the center of town, the pool is a part of what makes Piedmont such a special place and keeps our property values strong. The new competitive sports pool will: • Allow the 1,000 students currently involved in Piedmont Scouting to complete their mandatory BSA swimming merit badges. Over the past 10 years, many hundreds of students have earned this badge at the Piedmont Pool. • Provide a place for advanced swim lessons and opportunities for our youth to learn valuable lifesaving and water safety skills. • Host the Piedmont High School swim and water polo teams – allowing these teams to practice and play close to home rather than commute to neighboring communities. • Be a venue for lifelong exercise and social interaction for lap and Masters swimmers. • • • The new recreational pool will: Include improved space for beginner swim lessons and safe water play. Provide a place where Piedmonters of all ages and swimming abilities can swim and socialize together on warm summer days. Allow senior citizens and lessabled residents to benefit from water exercise and strengthening classes; getting into the water will be aided by the new zero depth entry feature. We urge all our citizens to support this measure to upgrade this vital and nurturing community resource. Please vote Yes on UU. –Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke
articles.title: Plenty of reasons to Vote Yes on Measure UU

articles.text: Editor: The Piedmont pool is an important community resource and serves many groups within our town, including Scouting. Scouting BSA runs many different programs for both boys and girls from the ages of 6 to 18. An important part of these is water safety. Scouts use the pool for swim safety testing prior to going to summer camps. They earn merit badges including the Swimming Merit Badge and the Lifesaving Merit Badge. And many take lifeguard training and CPR at the pool. Learning to swim, learning about water safety, and generally having fun are all essential parts of scouting and life. Let’s rebuild the pool into something we can all be proud of for many generations to come just as Piedmonters did 50 years ago for us. Vote yes on Measure UU. –Glyn Burge

articles.text: Editor: First, I would like to thank the Piedmont Post for providing a forum for a lively but respectful exchange of views on Measure UU. However, I would like to disagree with the statement made by the Editor in last week’s paper that “the residents have spoken”. There are roughly 8,500 registered voters in Piedmont, and they will speak on November 3rd. On November 4th, we will know what they said. That is how the democratic process works. Until that time, any attempts to speak for them are purely opinions and should be treated as such. –Bob Morrison

One of the great advantages of Piedmont was that our children were able walk to school, to their friends’ homes, to sports team practices and to the pool. There was no need to be constantly in the car – carpooling and driving children from place to place as we did in Houston. Over the years, my children enjoyed recreational swim at the Piedmont pool, and I started my days with a 6 a.m. lap swim. When our first grandchild, Luke, was born, his first exposure to swimming was a parent-child swim class with me at the Piedmont pool. Luke continued using the pool at Piedmont High School where he was a member of the PHS water polo and swim teams. For the past six years, our 13-year-old granddaughter has been a member of the Piedmont Swim Team. With no pool to use in Piedmont, she and the team practice at pools in Emeryville, Alameda and Montclair. I’m now carpooling again! I know the important role that a swimming pool plays in the community and I am passionate about having a pool available to Piedmont residents and students attending Piedmont schools. I grew up spending my summers at the local public pool and eventually, during college summers, was employed as head lifeguard and director of the learn-to-swim program at the local public pool. Cavenaugh said that climate change is one of the biggest threats to our health and environment. She said that we “would have the greatest impact if we reduce our consumption, switch to 100 percent renewable energy sources, and walk, bike, take public transportation or drive an electric car.” McCarthy supported a conversation about a utility tax, but said it is not the right time to propose. “Piedmonters already pay a premium. I think it’s $6 a month for East Bay Community Energy for 100 percent renewable energy on our electrical appliances. I don’t see the necessity right now,” she said. 3. Beninati asked the candidates how Piedmont can add more affordable housing. Herrick started by saying she was a very strong advocate for affordable housing and said that she recognized Piedmont’s builtout characteristic. “We are basically horizontally-challenged. We’ve maxed out on the lots. Is there a way that for us to go up? And can we go up in areas that are more commercially oriented, like on Grand Avenue or in the center of town? That would preserve the residential flavor of the rest of our city,” she said. Cavenuagh said that, even though Piedmont is a small city, more needs to be done to provide affordable housing. “We are embarking on a process to reevaluate our plans for providing housing of all types, specifically meet our regional housing number allocation that comes from the state. This process is going to look at lot size minimums, (Accessory Dwelling Unit) guidelines, multi-family housing zoning and many other aspects of our housing element to identify options for new housing,” she said. McCarthy provided SOME statistics on Piedmont housing goals. “For 2007 to 2014, our number was 40 units, for 2015 to 2022, our [state] allocation is 60 units with 49 units already completed by the end of 2019. Most of those new units are Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU). It’s predicted in the next period our ask to Piedmont could be 180-600 units. We’re not going to get there with ADUs. We have to be creative, we have to look at multi-dwelling structures, maybe in commercial areas where there’s space,” she said. Bostrom said that it would have to be delicately decided. “It will change the look of this city forever,” she said. SUDOKU SOLUTION
