articles.text: Because of the current health pandemic, and to mitigate potential gatherings, only one polling precinct will be open in Piedmont this upcoming election. Customarily Piedmont has six voting locations during an election The Veterans’ Memorial Building will serve as the only voting location for in-person voting this election. Any resident of Alameda County can come to the Veterans Hall and cast a ballot, and any county resident, including Piedmonters, may drop off their absentee ballot with a precinct worker. The building will be open four consecutive days, from Saturday, October 31, through Tuesday, November 4. Hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. the first three days, and 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. on the official Election Day, November 3. Voters may also put their absentee ballots (Vote By Mail ballots) into the secure ballot box located on Highland Way near the two US. Post Office mailboxes. The deadline for ballots to be turned in is November 3 at 8 p.m. A complete list of voting locations in Alameda County is available online at: https://www. acgov.org/rov_app/pollinglist. The Alameda County Registrar of Voters began mailing Sample Ballot and Voter Information Guides to registered voters on September 24. Absentee ballots were mailed to Piedmont voters on Wednesday, October 7, and Sample Ballots were received at residences in Piedmont this past Saturday, October 10. If you have not received your absentee ballot or sample ballot by October 16, contact the registrar office at (510) 272-6933. This year’s General Election includes the election of two seats on Piedmont City Council and three seats on the School Board. Other noteworthy elections include the President of the United States, United States Representative, and state Assembly, as well as several statewide measures, special district measures, and two City of Piedmont measures: Measure TT (real estate transfer tax) and Measure UU (bond for new municipal pool). of experts here: public health experts, educators, and the parents. Bringing all those groups together, and finding a consensus to avoid conflict is what we need to continue to do,” he said. Incumbent Smegal said that reopening was not a decision the Board took lightly. “The board has met, not only in our regular meetings but in nine or 10 special board meetings to talk about reopening. When Alameda County gave the green light to do this phased reopening, we were ready,” she said. 4. When asked what the biggest challenge the board will face in the coming years, all candidates mentioned the pandemic, reopening, and budget concerns. Thigpen said the pandemic and the subsequent strain on the school district’s budget would prove the most challenging. “I think that we’re to have to make some tough decisions,” she said. Kelley agreed that public health and budget were of utmost concern. “I also would like to see the board work on expanding the opportunities for students who are outside of the norm on either end of that spectrum, for both special education and advanced learners,” he said. “They have a lot of commonalities in the services that they need. Early identification, curriculum differentiations, regular reevaluations. Making sure those kids are served best is a priority as well.” Smegal also cited reopening and budget concerns. “We really do need to focus on our students’ social and emotional needs and their mental health,” she added, and said that the pandemic may have exacerbated already existing issues in that sector. Titan agreed that the pandemic and schools reopening are the biggest concerns. “I would also look at the learning loss, try to measure it, and make sure that we’re fair between hybrid and 100 percent distance learning kids,” he said. He added that he would like to look at the outcome of kids after graduation. Cooper said that a collaborative school board will be paramount in addressing both reopening safety and budget concerns. “We’re faced with the challenges that are from the pandemic and opening schools safely to learning loss to the social and emotional wellbeing of our children to trying to rectify the racial inequities that have occurred. I think we’re going to have to be open-minded and willing to think outside the box,” she said.

articles.text: Jason Kelley, incumbent Cory Smegal, Hari Titan, Hilary Cooper, and Veronica Anderson Thigpen gave opening statements, respectively, as Piedmont Board of Education candidates. Questions were asked regarding inclusion within the school community, reopening schools, and safety among staff and students during the current health pandemic. The five candidates were asked a series of questions, with the order of responses rotated on each question. 1. The first question asked of candidates was how Piedmont schools can make the district environment welcome and safe for students in marginalized groups. Incumbent Smegal said the most important thing the district can do is “listen to the students’ needs.” “Until we can identify the problem and the causes of this marginalization, it’s hard to provide solutions,” she added, and pointed to two policies the board has passed recently to combat this issue. Titan said he would like to see a more diverse faculty. “I think having more adults who are in a position of authority, who may belong to the same protected class that the child is experiencing [isolation] from, then they can see that there are adults out there who will protect them and look out for their interests.” Thigpen suggested the adoption of an anti-racism curriculum across all grades. Incumbent Smegal said the most important thing the district can do is “listen to the students’ needs.” “Until we can identify the problem and the causes of this marginalization, it’s hard to provide solutions,” she added, and pointed to two policies the board has passed recently to combat this issue. Titan said he would like to see a more diverse faculty. “I think having more adults who are in a position of authority, who may belong to the same protected class that the child is experiencing [isolation] from, then they can see that there are adults out there who will protect them and look out for their interests.” Thigpen suggested the adoption of an anti-racism curriculum across all grades. She added that faculty would receive training as well, and that the district can create safe spaces that “would feel inclusive and welcoming for students of color and where they could meet up and feel a sense of community.” Cooper said that it is imperative students have role models that they can lean on. “I also think the mentor program that the Black Student Union and the Asian American Association started at Havens is a really wonderful example of reaching out to our students to make sure that they have role models that look like them and share similar culture that they can feel like their voices are heard and have somebody to lean on,” Cooper said. Kelley provided an anecdote. “I know what it’s like to feel marginalized in Piedmont schools. As a gay kid in the 1980s, I felt very alone, and I really wish I had a teacher or other adult to connect with and talk with about that,” he said. He agreed that diversifying the staff would be a good first step. “Finding ways to partner with neighboring districts, perhaps in extracurriculars and other activities so that our kids have a chance to interact with a broad range of students,” he added. 3. Candidates were then asked if they supported the vote to reopen schools in phase with special education students and K-2 students returning to in person first. Titan praised the board’s decision to reopen. “It’s not the same risk for everyone, as teachers have been saying in their negotiations with the school district. Giving parents this choice, parental choice between 100 percent distance learning and hybrid in classroom instruction is the right way to go. Parents and families know what’s best for them and this will allow this flexibility that is sorely needed right now,” he said. Cooper said that she felt confident that schools can be opened safely, noting that Alameda County COVID numbers have been consistent. For secondary students, she said she hopes “that the district will look at some kind of creative way to get those kids out in some kind of small group or pod or cohort where they can meet with wellness center counselors or some kind of teacher to just share feelings about how they’re doing.” Thgpen mentioned that communication between teachers and faculty is important, adding that everyone is eager to have students back in school safely. “I definitely agree with the approach of phasing it in and bringing in our youngest students first and making sure that our students that have learning differences also get to go back to school first. articles.text: Akebono Cherries along Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park T he Park Com mission revealed the 2020 Heritage Tree designations at their October 7 meeting. The Heritage Tree program was created in 2018 under the leadership of commissioner Jim Horner. In 2019, the commission selected five trees from more than a dozen submissions. This year, 11 nominations were received: 6 for single trees, and 5 for groups of trees, Horner explained. Submitted nominations were evaluated on their aesthetic, education, or historical metrics. Nominations must be trees situated on public property, such as parks, medians, and streets. After vetting by Public Works department arborists, qualifying trees are then forwarded to the commission for review and selection. “It’s a wonderful tradition, and a positive connection that the city makes with the residents all over Piedmont every spring,” Commission Chair Patty Dunlap said. Traditionally, winning trees are recognized on Arbor Day. Because of the current health pandemic, this year’s announcements were made six months later via teleconference application Zoom. Five trees were chosen this year. Commissioner Eileen Ruby nominated a multi-trunk Japanese Maple, prominently positioned at the entrance to the teahouse garden in Piedmont Park. Resident Tami Becker nominated a Coast Live Oak in Dracena Park. “It is a handsome, featured tree, and its prominence will become more dramatic and important as years go by,” Horner commented. Commissioner Brian Mahany nominated the Southern Magnolia in the Huntleigh/Hampton Triangle. A circle of Coast Redwoods at the Jerome Triangle. Resident Jennifer Marinelly nominated a grove of Coast Redwoods at the Jerome Triangle. “They’ve been growing strong since they were planted by [former Public Works Supervisor] Dave Frankel in 1991,” Horner explained. Resident Nancy McHugh nominated the Akebono Cherry trees along Cherry Walk in Piedmont Park. “We are excited for when we can all be together and have an appropriate celebration. These are beautiful selections,” Dunlap commented. Signage for the newly designated trees is underway, said Nancy Kent. A multi-trunk Japanese Maple in Piedmont Park. articles.text: PG&E may shut off power for some areas near Piedmont today Hot, dry and gusty weather is forecasted for later this week, leading to concerns of increased wildfire risks throughout Northern California over the next few days. Yesterday, Tuesday, October 13, the National Weather Service issued a Red Flag Warning, meaning wildfire risk is high through Friday morning, October 16 for higher elevation areas in the East Bay Hills. The Weather Service pointed to gusty winds moving from offshore paired with an extremely dry air mass moving from the south. Fire Chief Bret Black said earlier this week that the Red Flag Warning was expected considering weather patterns. “We are expecting dangerously low humidity and some significant winds for the rest of the week,” Black told the Post. PG&E said this week that some Alameda County residents were among 50,000 Northern California customers notified this week about a potential Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) starting today, Wednesday, October 14 due to wildfire risk. According to the power utility’s website as of press time, impacted areas include Oakland neighborhoods directly to the east of Piedmont, including Montclair. “These types of weather events can trigger a PSPS event; residents should stay informed by visiting PG&E’s website where they can update their emergency contact information for PG&E’s alerting system,” Black continued. He advised Piedmonters to check PG&E’s website, pge.com, for PSPS information. On Saturday, October 10, the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) put a “Spare the Air” alert into place for the following four days, but the alert was lifted on Monday, October 12. BAAQMD said that increased containment of the Glass Fire in the North Bay has resulted in less smoke in the overall region, although it did cause hazy skies in the Bay Area last weekend. The Glass Fire began early on September 27 and has burned over 67,000 acres in Napa and Sonoma counties. An estimated 1,555 structures have been destroyed. The fire, which has burned through many vineyards and wineries, was 96 percent contained as of yesterday. Back in the station Black noted that all Piedmont firefighters are back after helping fight huge wildfires elsewhere in the state. “Piedmont Fire Department is currently fully staffed; all of our mutual aid resources have returned,” Black said. “We intend to increase staffing for the elevated wildfire risk.” CalFire notes that wildfire risks remain throughout October and November. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. “In October and November, ‘above normal’ wildfire potential will persist until significant and sustained rain arrives,” Black said. “Residents are reminded to prepare for wildfire evacuation and have a Go Bag ready!” The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage on the City’s website, www.ReadyForWildfire.org.
articles.title: Heat, dry weather, wind this week raise wildfire concerns in N. Calif.

Back in the station Black noted that all Piedmont firefighters are back after helping fight huge wildfires elsewhere in the state. “Piedmont Fire Department is currently fully staffed; all of our mutual aid resources have returned,” Black said. “We intend to increase staffing for the elevated wildfire risk.” CalFire notes that wildfire risks remain throughout October and November. Some of the most devastating wildfires in California history, such as the 2018 Camp Fire, began in November. “In October and November, ‘above normal’ wildfire potential will persist until significant and sustained rain arrives,” Black said. “Residents are reminded to prepare for wildfire evacuation and have a Go Bag ready!” The Piedmont Fire Department encourages all residents to prepare for fire emergencies. Black recommends Piedmonters learn how to prevent wildfires by visiting the PFD webpage on the City’s website, www.ReadyForWildfire.org. Where in the World Are We? Standing on the fourth green of the world-famous Dino Golf Course in Woodside, California, Bob and Diane Coleman enjoy reading about Rev. William McNabb’s retirement from Piedmont Community Church as Maureen and Bill McNabb look on.
